Did you know that 2 out of 3 women who start Ozempic or Wegovy for weight loss quit within the first year?

Not because they wanted to. Because the bloating, the constipation, the nausea — it gets worse the longer you stay on it.

But here's the part nobody warns you about before you fill that first prescription...

The side effects aren't random. And they don't get better with time — they get worse. There's a specific reason for that, and a reason everything your doctor tells you to take for them doesn't work.

I know because I almost became one of the 2 out of 3.

My name is Dana. I'm 51. I started Mounjaro last May for weight loss. Not diabetes. The pants had stopped fitting. I'd stopped looking in mirrors, stopped saying yes to pool parties with my daughter's friends.

The first three months were incredible. I lost 34 pounds. My knees stopped aching on the stairs. I wore a sundress to my niece's wedding and my sister-in-law grabbed my arm and whispered "What are you doing? I need to start."

Then month four hit.

I stopped going to the bathroom. Not the way people mean when they say things slowed down. I mean it stopped. Three days. Then five. My stomach would bloat so bad by dinnertime that I looked six months pregnant. I could feel the pressure building under my ribs like something was stuck up there and couldn't move.

I stopped eating dinner. Told my husband I wasn't hungry. But I was. I just couldn't face another night on the couch with my waistband cutting into me while my stomach cramped and gurgled loud enough for him to hear from the other end of the sofa.

The mornings got worse than the nights. I'd wake up before anyone else and go straight to the bathroom. Sit there for twenty minutes hoping something would happen. Sometimes it did. Mostly it didn't. Then I'd get dressed and pretend everything was fine.

I bought Miralax and mixed it into Gatorade like I'd read on Reddit. It worked for three days, then stopped. I added magnesium citrate at bedtime. Nothing. Tried a probiotic my coworker swore by — $54 a month for a supplement that did absolutely nothing. Metamucil made the bloating worse. Gas-X was like throwing a cup of water on a house fire.

I had seven different bottles on my bathroom counter. My husband looked at them one morning and said "Babe, when did this happen?"

I didn't have an answer.

I mentioned it to my doctor at my next appointment. Told her I hadn't had a normal bowel movement in three weeks. That I'd stopped eating dinner. That I had seven different products on my counter and none of them were working.

She typed something into her laptop and said "Try increasing your fiber and make sure you're drinking enough water."

I was eating 30 grams of fiber a day. I was drinking 80 ounces of water. I wanted to scream.

Then I made the mistake I said I'd never make. I skipped a dose. Just one. Told myself I needed a break, just a few days to feel normal. By day three the bloating went down, I had a normal bowel movement for the first time in weeks, and I felt like a human being again.

Then I stepped on the scale. Up two pounds in four days.

I stood there doing the math. If I kept skipping doses every time the constipation got unbearable, I'd be right back where I started by winter. The body I'd spent nine months fighting to leave. The pants that didn't fit. Pool parties I'd dread again.

People who stop taking semaglutide or tirzepatide gain back more than half the weight they lost. Most of it starts coming back within eight weeks. The average person is right back where they started in under two years.

I was not going to let that happen. But I also couldn't keep living like this.

So that night I stopped scrolling Reddit for product recommendations and started reading actual research. I wanted to know WHY the constipation was getting worse instead of better. Why none of the seven bottles on my counter were doing anything.

I found an article by a gastroenterologist who specialized in motility — the way your stomach physically moves food through your body. She said something that made me want to throw every bottle on my counter in the garbage.

She said: the medication slows your stomach down on purpose. That's how it works. It keeps food in there longer so you eat less and feel full.

But when your stomach slows down that much, food doesn't just sit there quietly. Bacteria start breaking it down while it's still in the stomach. It ferments. That's the bloating, the gas, the pressure under your ribs. Your food is rotting in a stomach that's barely moving.

And every single thing I'd been taking?

Miralax pulls water into the colon. My problem wasn't in my colon. The food hadn't even gotten there yet.

Magnesium citrate does the same thing — stimulates contractions in the colon. Wrong organ. Same dead end.

Fiber was actually making it worse. It bulks up stool in the colon, but if food is fermenting in my stomach six feet upstream, adding bulk at the exit isn't helping.

And the probiotic was adding bacteria to my lower gut. I didn't need more bacteria. I needed food to stop sitting in my stomach long enough for bacteria to eat it in the first place.

Seven products. Not one of them aimed at where the problem actually was.

I started looking for what works on the stomach — not the colon.

The first thing I found was a compound called apigenin. It's concentrated in celery juice extract. Research showed it supports stomach motility — helps the muscles that push food through your stomach actually do their job. Not by forcing a contraction like a laxative. By waking up the process the medication was suppressing.

Then I found chlorophyllin. When food ferments in the stomach it produces gases — the bloating, the pressure, the smell. Chlorophyllin doesn't mask the gas. It neutralizes it before it builds.

And the third was a specific kind of prebiotic fiber that feeds the good bacteria in the colon. Because the colon does still need support. It's just not where the main problem is.

I needed something that did all three. Wakes up the stomach. Handles the fermentation. Supports the colon downstream. I couldn't find anything that combined them. Everything had one piece — a motility supplement, or a gas product, or a fiber. Never all three.

Then I found a small company called Motilli.

Celery juice gummies. Apigenin from celery juice extract. Chlorophyllin. Prebiotic fiber. All three in one gummy.

I almost didn't order it. After seven failures, you stop trusting labels. But it cost less than the probiotic that did nothing. So I figured I had less to lose than the 34 pounds I was trying to keep off.

The first five days — nothing. I almost put them in the drawer with everything else.

Day seven I woke up and went to the bathroom. It was normal. Like before Mounjaro. I sat there for a second after because I wasn't sure I believed it.

By week two the bloating started going down. Not gone. But I ate dinner with my husband for the first time in six weeks without unbuttoning my jeans after.

By week four I just stopped thinking about it. I went to the bathroom in the morning like a normal person and got on with my day. The pressure under my ribs was gone. I ate three meals again. My husband noticed before I said anything — he said "You seem like yourself again." I didn't even know I hadn't been.

My sister-in-law — the one from the wedding — she'd started Mounjaro two months after me. She called me crying because she hadn't had a bowel movement in six days and her doctor told her to try more fiber and drink more water. I told her to stop buying fiber and order what I'd been taking. She texted me four days later: "I don't know what you gave me but I need to order my own."

I'm down 52 pounds now. Ten months on Mounjaro. Still taking my gummy every day.

I'm not one of the 2 out of 3.

But I almost was. And the only difference is that I stopped treating the wrong part of my body and started treating the right one.

You don't need to quit your medication. And another laxative isn't going to fix it. Neither is more fiber.

You need to stop treating your colon and start treating your stomach.

Last Saturday my daughter had a pool party. I stayed the whole afternoon. Ate a burger off the grill. Didn't think about my stomach once.

Fifty-two pounds down. Motilli.

My husband stopped kissing me the month I lost 26 pounds.

Not all at once. He just started aiming for my forehead instead of my mouth. And I let him. Because I knew what he'd find if he got any closer.

Three months on Mounjaro. Down 26 pounds. Two pant sizes gone. My doctor kept saying "incredible."

And I was rotting from the inside out.

Around week five, the burps started. Not normal burps. These tasted like something had crawled inside me and died. Sulfur — hot, thick, completely unpredictable. Mid-conversation at dinner. Mid-kiss goodnight. It would just come, and there was nothing I could do except swallow it back down and pray nobody noticed.

I'd never had a stomach problem in 46 years. Not once. My gut was the one part of my body I never thought about. Six weeks into Mounjaro, I woke up at 2am with acid crawling up my throat so bad I drove to Walgreens in my pajamas and bought Tums for the first time in my life.

I started chewing gum constantly. Mints in every pocket, every purse, my car. I'd excuse myself mid-conversation to let one out in private, then come back smiling like nothing happened.

Greg never said a word. That was worse. It wasn't a fight. It was his hand not reaching for mine on the couch. The forehead kiss replacing the real one — and both of us pretending that was normal.

My thirteen-year-old walked in one night while I was rinsing my mouth at the sink. "Mom, are you okay? Your breath smells weird." I told her I ate something bad. I was lying to my daughter about my own body.

I stopped accepting dinner invitations. Started eating alone in the kitchen after everyone finished — window open, praying nothing came up while my kids were still in the house.

That's the toll nobody warns you about. They show you the before-and-after photos. They don't show you the woman eating alone because she can't sit at the table with people she loves.

One night I sat on the edge of the bathtub and made myself be honest.

Option one: stay on Mounjaro. Keep losing weight. Keep the mints, the lies, the forehead kisses.

Option two: quit. Watch the 26 pounds come back.

Disappear physically or disappear from the people around me.

I refuse to believe those are the only two doors.

I didn't know what the third one was. But I knew who might.

My sister-in-law Rachel is a pharmacist — the kind who actually reads the research and knows what interacts with what. She's who our family calls before anyone takes anything. I called her on a Tuesday night, close to tears.

She wasn't even surprised.

What she told me made me furious. Not at her. At everything I'd been doing for the past three months.

GLP-1 medications slow down gastric emptying. That's the whole point — that's how they suppress appetite.

But when food sits in your stomach longer than your body is designed for, bacteria go to work on it. They ferment it. Like a traffic jam that turns into a junkyard.

That fermentation is what produces hydrogen sulfide gas.

That's the sulfur. That's what I'd been tasting at the back of my throat for three months while I chewed mints like they were going to save my marriage.

And the pressure from food sitting too long pushes acid up into your esophagus. That's the reflux. That's why I suddenly had heartburn at 46 after a lifetime of nothing.

All of it — the sulfur, the acid, the 2am Walgreens runs — coming from the same place. Food not moving.

I told Rachel about the Gas-X, the Tums, the Pepcid, the Pepto. She was quiet for a second. Then: "None of those touch motility. Not one."

Gas-X breaks up air bubbles — but my problem wasn't trapped air, it was fermentation gas being produced continuously. Like running a fan in a room where the fire's still burning. Tums and Pepcid managed the acid but didn't touch the pressure pushing it up. And Pepto — the one thing that actually helped the sulfur — my doctor said I couldn't take long-term.

Four products. All working below the problem. None of them going where it starts.

I'd spent three months paying the toll — pulling away from the people I love — while treating symptoms of something I didn't even understand.

Rachel wasn't done. She said the real problem isn't just one thing going wrong. It's three. And they feed each other.

She said the food not moving is the big one — everything cascades from there. But even once you get things moving, you've got hydrogen sulfide that's built up and needs to be neutralized. And below the stomach, everything's backed up too. Get the stomach going but leave the intestines sitting still, she said, and you've just moved the traffic jam.

Nothing I'd tried went after more than one of those. And you can't fix one and leave the others running.

I asked her what to take. She wouldn't tell me. She said to look for something that addresses all three — and to be careful, because most of what's out there was built for a normal gut, not one on a GLP-1.

That night, after the kids went to bed, I started searching.

I typed in "natural motility support" and fell into a rabbit hole of research papers I barely understood. But one compound kept surfacing — celery juice extract. The researched, supplemental form. Study after study showed it helped wake up the stomach's natural contractions — nudging the conveyor belt from a dead stop back to a slow crawl. Not fighting the medication. Just keeping things from going completely still.

That was my sulfur. Food sitting and rotting because nothing was telling my stomach to move it along.

I bookmarked everything and went to bed.

Three nights later I went back to it. Rachel said the gas needs to be dealt with — not masked. I searched for anything that targets hydrogen sulfide directly and found chlorophyll. Not the stuff from high school biology. A supplemental form that binds to sulfide compounds before they ever reach your throat. Goes after the molecule that makes the smell.

Every mint I'd chewed. Every time I'd turned my head away from Greg. That was masking. This was actually stopping it.

The last piece clicked the following week. I'd been so focused on the stomach that I almost missed it — if you get things moving up top but everything below is still backed up, you haven't solved anything. I needed fiber, but not the bulking kind, which could actually make things worse when your gut's already slow. The research kept pointing to prebiotic fiber — the type that feeds beneficial bacteria in the lower tract and keeps everything clearing.

Now I knew what I was looking for. I spent the next two nights trying to find something — anything — that actually combined all three.

Magnesium citrate was the first thing everyone online recommended. I'd already been taking it. Helped with constipation, sure. But it didn't touch the sulfur or the motility problem. Like mopping the floor while the sink's still overflowing.

Enzyme blends looked promising until I realized they break food down but don't do anything about the fact that food isn't moving in the first place. Probiotics — every single one was designed for a normal gut. Not one built for what a GLP-1 actually does to your stomach.

And the few products with one of the right ingredients? Wrong doses. Unstandardized extracts. One celery juice capsule had so little extract it would've taken eight pills a day to match the research.

Every time I thought I'd found it, something was wrong. I started wondering if what Rachel described even existed as an actual product. Maybe the science was right but nobody had put it together yet.

I was about to close my laptop — genuinely ready to call it — when I found a small company called Motilli. Celery juice-based gummy made specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. Not a general digestive supplement with a new label. Actually built for what these medications do to your gut.

I opened the ingredient panel and checked it against everything I'd spent two weeks learning. Celery juice extract — there, at a real dose. Chlorophyll — there. Prebiotic fiber — there. All three, in the forms and concentrations that actually matched the research.

Sugar-free gummy. Green apple. Less than what I'd been spending on mints and Tums that weren't solving anything.

I ordered a bottle. If this didn't work, I was calling my prescriber the following Monday and telling her I was done.

The package arrived on a Thursday. I chewed two gummies before breakfast, put the bottle next to the coffee maker, and told myself not to expect anything.

I'd been disappointed too many times.

Nothing the first two days. Nothing on day three.

Day four — the burps after lunch were softer. The sulfur edge was fading. Not gone. But fading. More like a normal burp than that hot, rotten wave I'd been bracing for every time I opened my mouth.

By the end of week two, I went an entire Saturday without a single one. I didn't realize it until brushing my teeth that night — I hadn't thought about my breath once all day. I'd eaten lunch at the kitchen table with my family. Not alone by the window. At the table.

Week three I started sleeping through the night. By week five, I stopped buying Tums. At my eight-week check-in, my doctor pulled up the ingredient profile and said, "This actually makes sense for what these medications do."

But here's the moment I keep coming back to.

About six weeks in. Greg and I were watching TV. A Tuesday. He leaned over and kissed me. Not on the forehead. On the mouth. Like it was nothing. Like it was just what you do when you're sitting next to someone you love.

He didn't hold his breath. He didn't pull away. He just kissed me and went back to the show.

I went to the bathroom and cried. Not because anything dramatic happened. Because something normal happened. And I'd forgotten what normal felt like.

That's what the toll had actually been taking from me. Not just comfort. Not just convenience. The tiny ordinary moments that hold a marriage together. A kiss that means nothing and everything at the same time.

I sat on the bathroom floor for a while after that.

I told my friend Dana — same sulfur on Wegovy for months. She ordered that night without asking what was in it. Eleven days later she called me from a restaurant. I could hear her boyfriend in the background. "This is the first time I've eaten in public since March." She was crying a little. I understood why.

My mom started Zepbound and I sent her a bottle before she even had her first side effect. Two weeks later: "Order me three more."

My cousin Allie's story is the one that gets me. She'd quit Mounjaro entirely because of the burps. Gained back 19 pounds. She went back on with the gummies from day one. Five weeks in — down 11 pounds, zero sulfur burps. She texted me: "I didn't know you could do this medication without the suffering part."

I'm still on Mounjaro. Still losing weight. And I'm no longer paying for it with my marriage, my confidence, or my ability to sit in a room without an exit plan.

If you know what sulfur tastes like at the back of your throat — if you've been declining invitations, eating alone, lying about your breath — hear this.

You are not someone who has to choose between the weight loss and the people you love. That was never a real choice. It was a toll you were paying because every solution you tried was built for a different problem.

Your medication is doing exactly what it was designed to do. Your gut just needs help keeping up — something for motility, something for the gas, something to keep things clearing. Three things working together.

Your family doesn't need you smaller. They need you present. At the table. Kissing them goodnight without doing math about how close is too close.

Every week you spend managing this with products that weren't built for what's actually happening is another week of paying a toll you were never supposed to pay.

I got back the version of myself that eats at the table. That sits close to people without thinking about it. That gets kissed on the mouth on a random Tuesday like it's nothing.

I think you can get her back too.

She told me she had a spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she'd gone.

Day three she texted: "Nothing yet."

Day ten: "I went this morning. On my own. No Miralax. No enema. Just went."

Karen didn't.

And she's back at the baseball games.

My husband stopped kissing me the month I lost 26 pounds.

Not all at once. He just started aiming for my forehead instead of my mouth. And I let him. Because I knew what he'd find if he got any closer.

Three months on Mounjaro. Down 26 pounds. Two pant sizes gone. My doctor kept saying "incredible."

And I was rotting from the inside out.

Around week five, the burps started. Not normal burps. These tasted like something had crawled inside me and died. Sulfur — hot, thick, completely unpredictable. Mid-conversation at dinner. Mid-kiss goodnight. It would just come, and there was nothing I could do except swallow it back down and pray nobody noticed.

I'd never had a stomach problem in 46 years. Not once. My gut was the one part of my body I never thought about. Six weeks into Mounjaro, I woke up at 2am with acid crawling up my throat so bad I drove to Walgreens in my pajamas and bought Tums for the first time in my life.

I started chewing gum constantly. Mints in every pocket, every purse, my car. I'd excuse myself mid-conversation to let one out in private, then come back smiling like nothing happened.

Greg never said a word. That was worse. It wasn't a fight. It was his hand not reaching for mine on the couch. The forehead kiss replacing the real one — and both of us pretending that was normal.

My thirteen-year-old walked in one night while I was rinsing my mouth at the sink. "Mom, are you okay? Your breath smells weird." I told her I ate something bad. I was lying to my daughter about my own body.

I stopped accepting dinner invitations. Started eating alone in the kitchen after everyone finished — window open, praying nothing came up while my kids were still in the house.

That's the toll nobody warns you about. They show you the before-and-after photos. They don't show you the woman eating alone because she can't sit at the table with people she loves.

One night I sat on the edge of the bathtub and made myself be honest.

Option one: stay on Mounjaro. Keep losing weight. Keep the mints, the lies, the forehead kisses.

Option two: quit. Watch the 26 pounds come back.

Disappear physically or disappear from the people around me.

I refuse to believe those are the only two doors.

I didn't know what the third one was. But I knew who might.

My sister-in-law Rachel is a pharmacist — the kind who actually reads the research and knows what interacts with what. She's who our family calls before anyone takes anything. I called her on a Tuesday night, close to tears.

She wasn't even surprised.

What she told me made me furious. Not at her. At everything I'd been doing for the past three months.

GLP-1 medications slow down gastric emptying. That's the whole point — that's how they suppress appetite.

But when food sits in your stomach longer than your body is designed for, bacteria go to work on it. They ferment it. Like a traffic jam that turns into a junkyard.

That fermentation is what produces hydrogen sulfide gas.

That's the sulfur. That's what I'd been tasting at the back of my throat for three months while I chewed mints like they were going to save my marriage.

And the pressure from food sitting too long pushes acid up into your esophagus. That's the reflux. That's why I suddenly had heartburn at 46 after a lifetime of nothing.

All of it — the sulfur, the acid, the 2am Walgreens runs — coming from the same place. Food not moving.

I told Rachel about the Gas-X, the Tums, the Pepcid, the Pepto. She was quiet for a second. Then: "None of those touch motility. Not one."

Gas-X breaks up air bubbles — but my problem wasn't trapped air, it was fermentation gas being produced continuously. Like running a fan in a room where the fire's still burning. Tums and Pepcid managed the acid but didn't touch the pressure pushing it up. And Pepto — the one thing that actually helped the sulfur — my doctor said I couldn't take long-term.

Four products. All working below the problem. None of them going where it starts.

I'd spent three months paying the toll — pulling away from the people I love — while treating symptoms of something I didn't even understand.

Rachel wasn't done. She said the real problem isn't just one thing going wrong. It's three. And they feed each other.

She said the food not moving is the big one — everything cascades from there. But even once you get things moving, you've got hydrogen sulfide that's built up and needs to be neutralized. And below the stomach, everything's backed up too. Get the stomach going but leave the intestines sitting still, she said, and you've just moved the traffic jam.

Nothing I'd tried went after more than one of those. And you can't fix one and leave the others running.

I asked her what to take. She wouldn't tell me. She said to look for something that addresses all three — and to be careful, because most of what's out there was built for a normal gut, not one on a GLP-1.

That night, after the kids went to bed, I started searching.

I typed in "natural motility support" and fell into a rabbit hole of research papers I barely understood. But one compound kept surfacing — celery juice extract. The researched, supplemental form. Study after study showed it helped wake up the stomach's natural contractions — nudging the conveyor belt from a dead stop back to a slow crawl. Not fighting the medication. Just keeping things from going completely still.

That was my sulfur. Food sitting and rotting because nothing was telling my stomach to move it along.

I bookmarked everything and went to bed.

Three nights later I went back to it. Rachel said the gas needs to be dealt with — not masked. I searched for anything that targets hydrogen sulfide directly and found chlorophyll. Not the stuff from high school biology. A supplemental form that binds to sulfide compounds before they ever reach your throat. Goes after the molecule that makes the smell.

Every mint I'd chewed. Every time I'd turned my head away from Greg. That was masking. This was actually stopping it.

The last piece clicked the following week. I'd been so focused on the stomach that I almost missed it — if you get things moving up top but everything below is still backed up, you haven't solved anything. I needed fiber, but not the bulking kind, which could actually make things worse when your gut's already slow. The research kept pointing to prebiotic fiber — the type that feeds beneficial bacteria in the lower tract and keeps everything clearing.

Now I knew what I was looking for. I spent the next two nights trying to find something — anything — that actually combined all three.

Magnesium citrate was the first thing everyone online recommended. I'd already been taking it. Helped with constipation, sure. But it didn't touch the sulfur or the motility problem. Like mopping the floor while the sink's still overflowing.

Enzyme blends looked promising until I realized they break food down but don't do anything about the fact that food isn't moving in the first place. Probiotics — every single one was designed for a normal gut. Not one built for what a GLP-1 actually does to your stomach.

And the few products with one of the right ingredients? Wrong doses. Unstandardized extracts. One celery juice capsule had so little extract it would've taken eight pills a day to match the research.

Every time I thought I'd found it, something was wrong. I started wondering if what Rachel described even existed as an actual product. Maybe the science was right but nobody had put it together yet.

I was about to close my laptop — genuinely ready to call it — when I found a small company called Motilli. Celery juice-based gummy made specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. Not a general digestive supplement with a new label. Actually built for what these medications do to your gut.

I opened the ingredient panel and checked it against everything I'd spent two weeks learning. Celery juice extract — there, at a real dose. Chlorophyll — there. Prebiotic fiber — there. All three, in the forms and concentrations that actually matched the research.

Sugar-free gummy. Green apple. Less than what I'd been spending on mints and Tums that weren't solving anything.

I ordered a bottle. If this didn't work, I was calling my prescriber the following Monday and telling her I was done.

The package arrived on a Thursday. I chewed two gummies before breakfast, put the bottle next to the coffee maker, and told myself not to expect anything.

I'd been disappointed too many times.

Nothing the first two days. Nothing on day three.

Day four — the burps after lunch were softer. The sulfur edge was fading. Not gone. But fading. More like a normal burp than that hot, rotten wave I'd been bracing for every time I opened my mouth.

By the end of week two, I went an entire Saturday without a single one. I didn't realize it until brushing my teeth that night — I hadn't thought about my breath once all day. I'd eaten lunch at the kitchen table with my family. Not alone by the window. At the table.

Week three I started sleeping through the night. By week five, I stopped buying Tums. At my eight-week check-in, my doctor pulled up the ingredient profile and said, "This actually makes sense for what these medications do."

But here's the moment I keep coming back to.

About six weeks in. Greg and I were watching TV. A Tuesday. He leaned over and kissed me. Not on the forehead. On the mouth. Like it was nothing. Like it was just what you do when you're sitting next to someone you love.

He didn't hold his breath. He didn't pull away. He just kissed me and went back to the show.

I went to the bathroom and cried. Not because anything dramatic happened. Because something normal happened. And I'd forgotten what normal felt like.

That's what the toll had actually been taking from me. Not just comfort. Not just convenience. The tiny ordinary moments that hold a marriage together. A kiss that means nothing and everything at the same time.

I sat on the bathroom floor for a while after that.

I told my friend Dana — same sulfur on Wegovy for months. She ordered that night without asking what was in it. Eleven days later she called me from a restaurant. I could hear her boyfriend in the background. "This is the first time I've eaten in public since March." She was crying a little. I understood why.

My mom started Zepbound and I sent her a bottle before she even had her first side effect. Two weeks later: "Order me three more."

My cousin Allie's story is the one that gets me. She'd quit Mounjaro entirely because of the burps. Gained back 19 pounds. She went back on with the gummies from day one. Five weeks in — down 11 pounds, zero sulfur burps. She texted me: "I didn't know you could do this medication without the suffering part."

I'm still on Mounjaro. Still losing weight. And I'm no longer paying for it with my marriage, my confidence, or my ability to sit in a room without an exit plan.

If you know what sulfur tastes like at the back of your throat — if you've been declining invitations, eating alone, lying about your breath — hear this.

You are not someone who has to choose between the weight loss and the people you love. That was never a real choice. It was a toll you were paying because every solution you tried was built for a different problem.

Your medication is doing exactly what it was designed to do. Your gut just needs help keeping up — something for motility, something for the gas, something to keep things clearing. Three things working together.

Your family doesn't need you smaller. They need you present. At the table. Kissing them goodnight without doing math about how close is too close.

Every week you spend managing this with products that weren't built for what's actually happening is another week of paying a toll you were never supposed to pay.

I got back the version of myself that eats at the table. That sits close to people without thinking about it. That gets kissed on the mouth on a random Tuesday like it's nothing.

I think you can get her back too.

If you're on Ozempic, Wegovy, or Mounjaro and your stomach feels like it's full of cement, you can't stop burping sulfur, and you haven't had a normal bowel movement in weeks, I need you to hear this.

Because what I'm about to tell you is going to make you furious.

Here's what's happening right now:

One — The medication that's finally silencing your food noise is quietly wrecking your digestion from the top down. Not just "causing constipation." Something deeper.

Two — When you bring it up to your doctor, they're going to tell you to take Miralax and drink more water.

And three — There's a reason that advice doesn't work. And a reason nobody's telling you why.

I know this because I've watched it happen from the other side of the exam room.

I've been a nurse for 23 years. I've seen things that would make you lose sleep. But the thing I can't stop thinking about is a 58-year-old woman named Karen who sat on the exam table in our clinic and cried because she hadn't had a bowel movement in eleven days.

Let me tell you what happened to her.

She'd been on Wegovy for five months. Down 31 pounds. Bloodwork was beautiful. A1C improved. Blood pressure down. On paper, she was a textbook success.

I took her vitals and asked the standard questions. She answered everything fine until I asked, "Any digestive issues?"

And she just... stopped talking. Looked at the floor. Then looked at me with this expression I've seen a thousand times — the one where someone is deciding whether to tell the truth or say what they think the doctor wants to hear.

"I haven't gone to the bathroom in eleven days," she said.

I put down my clipboard.

She started talking fast, the way people do when they've been holding something in. The bloating so severe she couldn't button her pants. The sulfur burps that smelled like rotten eggs — so bad her grandson had commented on her breath at his baseball game in front of the whole bleacher section. The pressure in her stomach that kept her up at night. The feeling of food from dinner still sitting there the next morning, like a brick that wouldn't dissolve.

She told me about the enemas. Plural. That she'd given herself one at a gas station bathroom during a road trip because the pain was a ten out of ten and she couldn't make it to her daughter's house.

She told me about her medicine cabinet. Miralax. Dulcolax. Colace. Mag citrate. Fiber gummies. Senna. Smooth Move tea. Prune juice she hid behind the orange juice.

She told me she had a spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she'd gone.

Then she said the thing I hear from every one of these women:

"But I've lost 31 pounds. So I just deal with it."

The medication is giving her the body she's wanted for thirty years. But she's too sick to enjoy living in it.

Sound familiar?

The doctor spent nine minutes with her. I know because I checked.

He told Karen that constipation was a very common side effect. Asked if she was drinking enough water. Suggested increasing her fiber and trying Miralax.

Karen looked at him and said, "I've been taking Miralax every day for three months."

He paused. Typed something into the chart. Said they could try Linzess or consider lowering her dose.

Karen's face went white. "Lower my dose? I've lost thirty-one pounds."

Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three working together.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyll. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber. I checked each ingredient against the studies I'd been reading for three nights. Motility support. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three. At concentrations that matched the research.

I called her the next day. She'd stopped coming to our clinic — I wasn't surprised. I told her I'd found something I wanted her to try. Didn't oversell it. Just said it worked on the stomach instead of the colon, and I thought it was worth thirty days.

She went to her grandson's next game. Stayed the whole time.

My wife hasn't suggested we go anywhere in four months. Not dinner. Not the farmers market she used to drag me to every Saturday morning. Not even her sister's place. And they used to talk every single day.

I don't think she knows I've been keeping track.

She started Mounjaro last September. Lost 30 pounds by Christmas and I'd never seen her that happy. She bought new jeans for the first time in years. Actual jeans, not the stretchy ones. We went to a holiday party and she wanted to stay late. That never happens.

Then around January something shifted.

She stopped finishing meals. Started excusing herself from the table halfway through dinner. I'd hear her in the bathroom and I knew she wasn't sick -- not the kind of sick where you call someone. But something was wrong and she wasn't going to tell me what.

I found her one night sitting on the edge of the bathtub. Like 11pm. Phone in her lap. She was googling "is it normal to not go to the bathroom for 8 days." She closed the screen the second she saw me standing there. Said she was fine.

She wasn't fine.

The woman I married planned things. She'd text her friends, book restaurants, tell me we were doing something Saturday and I'd just show up. That was how we worked. Twenty-three years that was how we worked.

Now she cancels everything. Her friend Diane texted about lunch last week and I watched her type "can't make it, not feeling great" without even looking up from the couch. Diane texts every couple weeks now instead of every couple days. I don't think my wife has noticed that yet.

She wears the same three outfits. She used to spend twenty minutes deciding what to wear for a Saturday errand run. Now she grabs whatever's on top of the pile. I found the second pair of new jeans she bought in the back of the closet. Tags still on.

I used to come home and she'd already be in the kitchen. Music going, something on the stove, talking about her day before I got my shoes off. Now she's on the couch with a heating pad on her stomach and the TV on but she's not really watching it. She's just sitting there waiting for the discomfort to stop. Sometimes I stand in the hallway for a second before I walk in because I don't know what to say to her anymore.

The worst part is the look she gets after she eats. This kind of... bracing. Like she's waiting for something bad to start. She takes four or five bites and pushes her plate forward an inch and says she's full. She's not full. She's scared of what comes next.

I watched her try everything. Miralax twice a day. That fiber powder she stirred into her water every morning, the one that turns it kind of orange. Probiotic gummies her coworker told her about. She drank so much water I thought she was training for something.

None of it did anything. She'd try something for a week, maybe two, get her hopes up a little. Then quietly stop buying it. I could always tell when another one failed because she'd go a little quieter for a day or two. Like she'd used up her last bit of hope on it and just... didn't have any more to spend.

Her gastroenterologist told her to eat smaller meals and stay hydrated. I almost said something right there in the office. She's barely eating at ALL. How is eating less the answer.

I had two choices. Keep watching her turn into somebody I barely recognized. Or figure out what was actually happening to her.

She wasn't going to do it herself. She'd already decided this was just what the medication cost. The trade-off. I wasn't ready to accept that.

My buddy Dave is a pharmacist. We were at his place for a cookout in February and I brought it up while we were standing by the grill. Told him about the constipation, the bloating, all of it.

He said something I didn't expect. Said "Everything she's taking works on the end of the line. But her medication put the brakes on at the beginning."

I went home that night and I couldn't sleep. Just sat in the living room reading on my phone for like three hours.

Turns out GLP-1 medications -- Mounjaro, Ozempic, all of them -- they work partly by slowing the stomach down. That's actually how they reduce appetite. The stomach basically stops pushing food through at a normal speed.

Think of it like a parking brake. The medication pulls the parking brake on the stomach. Food comes in but it just sits there. Doesn't move. It ferments. That's the bloating. The nausea. The constipation. The sulfur burps she thought I didn't know about.

And here's what kept me up. Everything she'd been buying -- the Miralax, the fiber, the probiotics -- all of it works on the colon. Very end of the digestive system. Six feet downstream from where the problem actually is.

That's like calling a tow truck to the exit of a highway when the car broke down at the on-ramp. You can send ten tow trucks. They're all in the wrong place.

Miralax. Wrong location. Fiber. Wrong location. Probiotics -- they don't even touch the stomach.

No wonder nothing worked. Not for her. Not for anybody doing the same thing.

So I started looking for what actually works up there. What releases the parking brake.

First thing I found was celery juice extract. Not the TikTok thing. The actual extracted compound, something called apigenin. The research on it showed it helps with gastric motility -- basically means it wakes the stomach back up. Gets food moving from the top.

That's where I found chlorophyllin. It's a chlorophyll compound that breaks down the sulfur and gas from fermentation. Not a masking thing. Actually neutralizes it.

Last piece was the downstream backup. Even once the stomach wakes up and the gas gets handled, everything that was stuck behind it still needs to clear through. I started looking for a product that actually had all three. Most stuff I found had one. Maybe two. Nothing hit all of it.

Then I found this company called Motilli.

I almost kept scrolling. Another supplement website. But I checked what was in it. Celery juice extract. Chlorophyllin. Prebiotic fiber. All three. In a gummy.

I ordered a jar without telling her. Left it on the kitchen counter when it showed up.

She picked it up that evening. Looked at it. Looked at me. "What is this."

I said just try it. Two weeks. If nothing changes I'll drop it.

First week nothing happened. I could tell she wanted to tell me it was a waste of money but she held off.

Middle of the second week she mentioned -- almost like it was nothing -- that she'd gone to the bathroom that morning. First time in six days. She said it like a weather report. But I saw her face.

End of week three something bigger changed. She ate dinner. Not four bites. Dinner. Chicken, rice, green beans. Full plate. And she didn't do the bracing thing after. She just sat there talking to me about some show she wanted to watch. Like it was nothing.

But it wasn't nothing.

Around day 20 she had a rough night. Bloated. Uncomfortable. Almost stopped taking them. I told her give it the full month. She wasn't happy about it but she kept going.

Week four she texted Diane back. I know because I heard her laugh at something on her phone and asked who it was.

Month two she said we should try that new Italian place by the highway. She put on one of those new jeans. Spent fifteen minutes getting ready. I stood in the bedroom doorway watching her pick out a top and I had to leave the room for a second.

She ordered pasta. Ate the whole thing. Talked the entire time about her sister's kids and some trip she wanted to plan for the summer. I just sat there nodding because if I said anything I was going to lose it in the middle of an Olive Garden knockoff.

Her sister called me separately a couple weeks later. Asked what changed. Their mom noticed too. Apparently two women at her office who are on Ozempic asked what she was taking, and she brought the jar in to show them.

She told Diane about them last week. I overheard her on the phone saying "I know it sounds weird but just try them."

I don't know if this is the kind of thing people usually post. I'm really not a social media person. My daughter helped me figure out how to write this because she said people might need to hear it.

If you're watching someone you love shrink. And I don't mean the weight. I mean the actual person they are just getting... smaller. Quieter. Less there. And you feel like you can't do anything.

I got my wife back. Not the smaller version of her. The real one. The one who plans things and laughs too loud and spends fifteen minutes picking out a shirt for a Saturday night.

That's all I wanted. That's what this gave us.

Here's what's happening right now:

One — The medication that's finally helping you lose weight is doing something specific to the lining of your intestines. Not just "causing GI side effects." Something mechanical. Something no one has explained to you.

Two — When you bring it up to your doctor, they're going to tell you it's a common side effect and your body will adjust.

And three — There's a reason it hasn't adjusted. And a reason the Imodium keeps wearing off.

I know this because I've watched it happen from the other side of the pharmacy counter.

I've been a clinical pharmacist for 18 years. I've filled prescriptions for every class of drug you can name. But the thing I can't stop thinking about is a 46-year-old woman named Dana who came to my counter every single Monday morning for eleven months and bought Imodium.

Let me tell you what happened to her.

She'd been on Mounjaro for seven months. Down 37 pounds. Her A1C had improved. Her doctor was thrilled. On paper she was one of the success stories.

I handed her the Imodium the first few times without thinking about it. It's over the counter. People buy it. That's not unusual.

But by month four I started noticing. Every Monday. Same time. Same box. Sometimes two boxes. She'd grab a Liquid IV from the cooler, a box of Imodium, and pay without making eye contact.

One Monday she was buying her ninth box and I said something I probably shouldn't have. I said, "Dana, are you taking this every day?"

She looked at the counter. Then looked at me the way people do when they're deciding whether to lie or tell the truth to someone they see at a pharmacy counter.

"Every day since September," she said. "Sometimes twice."

I set down what I was doing.

It came out fast, the way it does when someone's been holding it in. The Thursday night injections. The Friday morning bathroom crisis that started like clockwork 14 hours later. The Saturdays she couldn't leave her house. The brunches she'd cancelled. The Target trip where she almost didn't make it — she abandoned her cart in the middle of the store and speed-walked to the bathroom. Made it. Barely. Cried in her car.

She told me about the emergency kit she keeps in her purse now. Extra underwear. Wet wipes. Imodium. "Like I'm packing a diaper bag for myself," she said. She tried to laugh when she said it. It didn't land.

She told me she moved her injection to Thursday night specifically so the worst days hit on Friday and Saturday when she can hide at home. She reorganized her entire week around being sick.

She told me about the BRAT diet she'd been eating for months. Rice. Bananas. Toast. Eggs. Nothing else. On a medication designed to help her lose weight, she was essentially starving herself out of fear that real food would set it off.

Then she said the thing I hear from all of them:

"But I've lost 37 pounds. So I just deal with it."

The medication is giving her the body she's wanted since her twenties. But she's too afraid to leave her house in it.

Sound familiar?

Her doctor spent maybe eight minutes with her at her last appointment. Told her diarrhea was a very common side effect. Her body was still adjusting. Suggested the BRAT diet — which she was already on. Suggested Imodium — which she was already taking daily.

Dana asked if there was anything else. He said they could consider lowering her dose.

Her face changed. "I've lost thirty-seven pounds."

He nodded. Follow up in eight weeks.

She told me this at the pharmacy counter on a Monday morning, holding her ninth box of Imodium, and she said, "He didn't hear me. None of them hear me."

I wanted to say something useful. Instead I said, "The Imodium should help manage it."

I already knew it wasn't managing anything. She'd been taking it daily for months and the diarrhea came back every single week.

But Dana broke something in me. Because she wasn't the first. She was the ninth. Ninth woman in my pharmacy buying Imodium on a weekly cycle that never ended. And I was the one handing it to them.

So I started researching. Not patient forums. Not the pamphlet that comes with every GLP-1 prescription — the one that says "GI side effects may occur" like that explains anything. The actual studies. The pharmacology.

And what I found at 2 AM on my night off, sitting at my kitchen table with three tabs of PubMed open, made me want to walk back to that counter and apologize to every woman I'd ever sold Imodium to without asking why they needed it every week.

Because the Imodium was never going to fix this. It was never designed to fix this.

Think of your intestinal wall as a tile floor. The cells are the tiles. Between each tile there's grout — proteins called tight junctions that seal the gaps between cells. When the seal is intact, fluid stays where it belongs. Your intestines process food normally.

GLP-1 medications activate receptors along your intestinal lining. That activation triggers inflammation. And when the lining gets inflamed, the grout starts breaking down. The seal between cells degrades. Gaps open up. Fluid that's supposed to stay inside the intestinal wall starts leaking through into the cavity.

Your body does the only thing it can with that fluid. It expels it. Urgently. That's the diarrhea.

And here's what nobody tells you: every injection re-triggers the inflammation. That's why it comes back every week like clockwork. The lining never fully heals before the next dose hits.

Now look at what Imodium actually does.

Imodium slows intestinal contractions. It tells the muscles in your gut to stop squeezing so hard. That buys you a few hours. But the seal is still broken. The fluid is still leaking. The lining is still inflamed. As soon as the Imodium wears off, the leaking resumes. Because Imodium doesn't touch the seal. It just slows down what your body does about the leak.

The BRAT diet reduces the volume of food hitting the intestines. Less input, less output. But the seal is still degraded. Even rice and bananas pass through a broken lining. You're not fixing anything — you're eating less so there's less to leak.

Probiotics colonize the gut. They can help with certain kinds of digestive disruption. But if the lining is inflamed and the tight junction proteins are degraded, adding more bacteria to a leaky system doesn't repair the grout. The structure is damaged. Bacteria can't fix a structural problem.

Pepto-Bismol coats the stomach lining. Different organ. Different surface. The inflammation is in the intestinal wall, not the stomach. Coating the stomach is putting a band-aid on your forehead when the cut is on your shin.

So the question became: what actually repairs the seal?

I spent three nights going through inflammatory pathway studies. Following citations. Three things kept showing up.

First — apigenin. A flavonoid concentrated in celery. It was showing up in studies on intestinal inflammation as an anti-inflammatory that specifically targets the pathway GLP-1 receptor activation triggers. Not a general anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen. Targeted. Calms the inflammation at the lining level. And when the inflammation reduces, the tight junction proteins start recovering. The grout starts filling back in.

That was the first piece. Address the inflammation that's degrading the seal.

But inflammation is only half the problem. Even after you calm the inflammatory response, the lining itself needs support to rebuild. Weeks or months of repeated damage mean the intestinal wall is depleted.

The second piece was chlorophyllin — a concentrated form of chlorophyll. It was appearing in gut barrier studies as a compound that supports intestinal wall integrity. Helps protect the lining cells themselves while the tight junctions recover. Like reinforcing the tiles while the grout sets.

Two pieces. But I kept reading. Because even with the inflammation calmed and the lining protected, the gut ecosystem underneath has been disrupted. Months of diarrhea have washed out the beneficial bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids — the compounds that fuel intestinal cells and keep the barrier strong from the inside.

The third piece was a specific type of soluble prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber doctors recommend for constipation — that would make diarrhea worse. This was low-bulk, gel-forming. Feeds the specific bacteria that produce butyrate, the primary fuel source for the cells that make up the intestinal wall. Strengthens the barrier from the inside out.

Three things. Calm the inflammation that's breaking the seal. Protect the lining while it recovers. Strengthen the barrier from the inside so it holds.

Inflammation control. Lining protection. Barrier rebuilding. All three working together.

That's when I understood why Dana's Imodium never stood a chance. It was slowing contractions in a system where the actual problem was a degraded seal. Like turning down the faucet pressure when the pipe has a crack in it. The water still leaks.

I started looking for something that combined all three. Found anti-inflammatory supplements with turmeric — wrong pathway, not targeted to intestinal tight junctions. Found chlorophyll drops with no anti-inflammatory component. Found prebiotic blends with insoluble fiber that would have made the diarrhea worse.

Everything had one piece. Nothing had all three in the right form.

Then I found a small company I'd never heard of. They'd built a gummy specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. Not a general gut health supplement rebranded with a new label.

Motilli.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyllin. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber. I checked each ingredient against the studies I'd been reading for three nights. Inflammation support. Lining protection. Barrier rebuilding. All three. In forms that matched what the research actually showed.

I bought two bottles that night. One for me to evaluate. One for Dana.

I called her the next morning. She'd stopped going to that Monday Imodium run about three weeks earlier — I'd noticed. Turns out she'd just switched to buying it at a different pharmacy because she was embarrassed I'd noticed the pattern.

I told her I'd found something I wanted her to try. Didn't oversell it. Just said it works on the intestinal lining instead of slowing the muscles, and I thought it was worth thirty days.

She was quiet. Then: "At this point I'll try anything that isn't another box of Imodium."

Two gummies a day. She started that Wednesday.

Day three she texted: "Still had it Friday morning."

I told her to give it time. This wasn't Imodium. It wasn't slowing anything down. It was repairing something. That takes longer than a few days.

Day eight: "Friday was... less. I went twice instead of six times. Could be nothing."

Day fourteen: "It's Saturday and I'm at Target."

That text hit different. Because I knew about the last time she was at Target. The abandoned cart. The speed walk. The car.

She was at Target on a Saturday. A post-injection Saturday. Voluntarily.

Week three — she went to brunch. First time since she'd started Mounjaro. She ordered eggs Benedict. Real food. Not rice. Not toast. She texted me a picture of the plate. No message. Just the plate.

I knew exactly what that picture meant.

Week four she had a setback. A bad Friday. Not as bad as before — three episodes instead of six — but enough to shake her. She almost stopped taking the gummies. I told her to keep going. Real repair isn't a straight line. The lining was still recovering.

Week five was better. Week six was the best she'd had since starting the medication.

Month two — Dana stopped buying Imodium entirely. Not from my pharmacy. Not from the other one. She didn't need it.

Her daughter noticed she was saying yes to things again. Saturday hikes. Errands that didn't require bathroom mapping. The kind of stuff that sounds tiny unless you've spent months not doing it.

"My daughter said I seem like myself again," she told me at the counter. She wasn't buying Imodium. She was picking up her Mounjaro refill. "She didn't know I'd been gone."

I've since shared the same research with six other patients. Quietly. On my own time. Between prescriptions. Every one had the same pattern — months of Imodium cycling, then steady improvement once something was finally repairing the lining instead of just slowing down the contractions.

Here's what I need you to hear — from a pharmacist who has been handing women Imodium every Monday morning for two years without asking the right questions:

Your doctors aren't wrong when they say diarrhea is a common side effect. They're right. But they're wrong about what's causing it. And because they think it's sensitivity or adjustment, every solution they offer manages the symptom instead of repairing the source.

Inflammation control. Lining protection. Barrier rebuilding. That's not a mystery. That's biology. And until something addresses all three, you can take Imodium every day for the rest of your prescription and still end up mapping bathrooms and cancelling Saturday plans.

You don't have to choose between the weight loss and your weekends.

You don't have to accept the Imodium cycle.

Dana didn't.

And she's back at Target on Saturdays.

That's all I wanted. That's what this gave us.

creative.body:
My husband stopped kissing me the month I lost 26 pounds.

Not all at once. He just started aiming for my forehead instead of my mouth. And I let him. Because I knew what he'd find if he got any closer.

Three months on Mounjaro. Down 26 pounds. Two pant sizes gone. My doctor kept saying "incredible."

And I was rotting from the inside out.

Around week five, the burps started. Not normal burps. These tasted like something had crawled inside me and died. Sulfur — hot, thick, completely unpredictable. Mid-conversation at dinner. Mid-kiss goodnight. It would just come, and there was nothing I could do except swallow it back down and pray nobody noticed.

I'd never had a stomach problem in 46 years. Not once. My gut was the one part of my body I never thought about. Six weeks into Mounjaro, I woke up at 2am with acid crawling up my throat so bad I drove to Walgreens in my pajamas and bought Tums for the first time in my life.

I started chewing gum constantly. Mints in every pocket, every purse, my car. I'd excuse myself mid-conversation to let one out in private, then come back smiling like nothing happened.

Greg never said a word. That was worse. It wasn't a fight. It was his hand not reaching for mine on the couch. The forehead kiss replacing the real one — and both of us pretending that was normal.

My thirteen-year-old walked in one night while I was rinsing my mouth at the sink. "Mom, are you okay? Your breath smells weird." I told her I ate something bad. I was lying to my daughter about my own body.

I stopped accepting dinner invitations. Started eating alone in the kitchen after everyone finished — window open, praying nothing came up while my kids were still in the house.

That's the toll nobody warns you about. They show you the before-and-after photos. They don't show you the woman eating alone because she can't sit at the table with people she loves.

One night I sat on the edge of the bathtub and made myself be honest.

Option one: stay on Mounjaro. Keep losing weight. Keep the mints, the lies, the forehead kisses.

Option two: quit. Watch the 26 pounds come back.

Disappear physically or disappear from the people around me.

I refuse to believe those are the only two doors.

I didn't know what the third one was. But I knew who might.

My sister-in-law Rachel is a pharmacist — the kind who actually reads the research and knows what interacts with what. She's who our family calls before anyone takes anything. I called her on a Tuesday night, close to tears.

She wasn't even surprised.

What she told me made me furious. Not at her. At everything I'd been doing for the past three months.

GLP-1 medications slow down gastric emptying. That's the whole point — that's how they suppress appetite.

But when food sits in your stomach longer than your body is designed for, bacteria go to work on it. They ferment it. Like a traffic jam that turns into a junkyard.

That fermentation is what produces hydrogen sulfide gas.

That's the sulfur. That's what I'd been tasting at the back of my throat for three months while I chewed mints like they were going to save my marriage.

And the pressure from food sitting too long pushes acid up into your esophagus. That's the reflux. That's why I suddenly had heartburn at 46 after a lifetime of nothing.

All of it — the sulfur, the acid, the 2am Walgreens runs — coming from the same place. Food not moving.

I told Rachel about the Gas-X, the Tums, the Pepcid, the Pepto. She was quiet for a second. Then: "None of those touch motility. Not one."

Gas-X breaks up air bubbles — but my problem wasn't trapped air, it was fermentation gas being produced continuously. Like running a fan in a room where the fire's still burning. Tums and Pepcid managed the acid but didn't touch the pressure pushing it up. And Pepto — the one thing that actually helped the sulfur — my doctor said I couldn't take long-term.

Four products. All working below the problem. None of them going where it starts.

I'd spent three months paying the toll — pulling away from the people I love — while treating symptoms of something I didn't even understand.

Rachel wasn't done. She said the real problem isn't just one thing going wrong. It's three. And they feed each other.

She said the food not moving is the big one — everything cascades from there. But even once you get things moving, you've got hydrogen sulfide that's built up and needs to be neutralized. And below the stomach, everything's backed up too. Get the stomach going but leave the intestines sitting still, she said, and you've just moved the traffic jam.

Nothing I'd tried went after more than one of those. And you can't fix one and leave the others running.

I asked her what to take. She wouldn't tell me. She said to look for something that addresses all three — and to be careful, because most of what's out there was built for a normal gut, not one on a GLP-1.

That night, after the kids went to bed, I started searching.

I typed in "natural motility support" and fell into a rabbit hole of research papers I barely understood. But one compound kept surfacing — celery juice extract. The researched, supplemental form. Study after study showed it helped wake up the stomach's natural contractions — nudging the conveyor belt from a dead stop back to a slow crawl. Not fighting the medication. Just keeping things from going completely still.

That was my sulfur. Food sitting and rotting because nothing was telling my stomach to move it along.

I bookmarked everything and went to bed.

Three nights later I went back to it. Rachel said the gas needs to be dealt with — not masked. I searched for anything that targets hydrogen sulfide directly and found chlorophyll. Not the stuff from high school biology. A supplemental form that binds to sulfide compounds before they ever reach your throat. Goes after the molecule that makes the smell.

Every mint I'd chewed. Every time I'd turned my head away from Greg. That was masking. This was actually stopping it.

The last piece clicked the following week. I'd been so focused on the stomach that I almost missed it — if you get things moving up top but everything below is still backed up, you haven't solved anything. I needed fiber, but not the bulking kind, which could actually make things worse when your gut's already slow. The research kept pointing to prebiotic fiber — the type that feeds beneficial bacteria in the lower tract and keeps everything clearing.

Now I knew what I was looking for. I spent the next two nights trying to find something — anything — that actually combined all three.

Magnesium citrate was the first thing everyone online recommended. I'd already been taking it. Helped with constipation, sure. But it didn't touch the sulfur or the motility problem. Like mopping the floor while the sink's still overflowing.

Enzyme blends looked promising until I realized they break food down but don't do anything about the fact that food isn't moving in the first place. Probiotics — every single one was designed for a normal gut. Not one built for what a GLP-1 actually does to your stomach.

And the few products with one of the right ingredients? Wrong doses. Unstandardized extracts. One celery juice capsule had so little extract it would've taken eight pills a day to match the research.

Every time I thought I'd found it, something was wrong. I started wondering if what Rachel described even existed as an actual product. Maybe the science was right but nobody had put it together yet.

I was about to close my laptop — genuinely ready to call it — when I found a small company called Motilli. Celery juice-based gummy made specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. Not a general digestive supplement with a new label. Actually built for what these medications do to your gut.

I opened the ingredient panel and checked it against everything I'd spent two weeks learning. Celery juice extract — there, at a real dose. Chlorophyll — there. Prebiotic fiber — there. All three, in the forms and concentrations that actually matched the research.

Sugar-free gummy. Green apple. Less than what I'd been spending on mints and Tums that weren't solving anything.

I ordered a bottle. If this didn't work, I was calling my prescriber the following Monday and telling her I was done.

The package arrived on a Thursday. I chewed two gummies before breakfast, put the bottle next to the coffee maker, and told myself not to expect anything.

I'd been disappointed too many times.

Nothing the first two days. Nothing on day three.

Day four — the burps after lunch were softer. The sulfur edge was fading. Not gone. But fading. More like a normal burp than that hot, rotten wave I'd been bracing for every time I opened my mouth.

By the end of week two, I went an entire Saturday without a single one. I didn't realize it until brushing my teeth that night — I hadn't thought about my breath once all day. I'd eaten lunch at the kitchen table with my family. Not alone by the window. At the table.

Week three I started sleeping through the night. By week five, I stopped buying Tums. At my eight-week check-in, my doctor pulled up the ingredient profile and said, "This actually makes sense for what these medications do."

But here's the moment I keep coming back to.

About six weeks in. Greg and I were watching TV. A Tuesday. He leaned over and kissed me. Not on the forehead. On the mouth. Like it was nothing. Like it was just what you do when you're sitting next to someone you love.

He didn't hold his breath. He didn't pull away. He just kissed me and went back to the show.

I went to the bathroom and cried. Not because anything dramatic happened. Because something normal happened. And I'd forgotten what normal felt like.

That's what the toll had actually been taking from me. Not just comfort. Not just convenience. The tiny ordinary moments that hold a marriage together. A kiss that means nothing and everything at the same time.

I sat on the bathroom floor for a while after that.

I told my friend Dana — same sulfur on Wegovy for months. She ordered that night without asking what was in it. Eleven days later she called me from a restaurant. I could hear her boyfriend in the background. "This is the first time I've eaten in public since March." She was crying a little. I understood why.

My mom started Zepbound and I sent her a bottle before she even had her first side effect. Two weeks later: "Order me three more."

My cousin Allie's story is the one that gets me. She'd quit Mounjaro entirely because of the burps. Gained back 19 pounds. She went back on with the gummies from day one. Five weeks in — down 11 pounds, zero sulfur burps. She texted me: "I didn't know you could do this medication without the suffering part."

I'm still on Mounjaro. Still losing weight. And I'm no longer paying for it with my marriage, my confidence, or my ability to sit in a room without an exit plan.

If you know what sulfur tastes like at the back of your throat — if you've been declining invitations, eating alone, lying about your breath — hear this.

You are not someone who has to choose between the weight loss and the people you love. That was never a real choice. It was a toll you were paying because every solution you tried was built for a different problem.

Your medication is doing exactly what it was designed to do. Your gut just needs help keeping up — something for motility, something for the gas, something to keep things clearing. Three things working together.

Your family doesn't need you smaller. They need you present. At the table. Kissing them goodnight without doing math about how close is too close.

Every week you spend managing this with products that weren't built for what's actually happening is another week of paying a toll you were never supposed to pay.

I got back the version of myself that eats at the table. That sits close to people without thinking about it. That gets kissed on the mouth on a random Tuesday like it's nothing.

I think you can get her back too.

Two pieces. But I kept reading.
