If you're on Ozempic, Wegovy, or Mounjaro and your stomach feels like it's full of cement, you can't stop burping sulfur, and you haven't had a normal bowel movement in weeks, I need you to hear this.

Because what I'm about to tell you is going to make you furious.

Here's what's happening right now:

One — The medication that's finally silencing your food noise is quietly wrecking your digestion from the top down. Not just "causing constipation." Something deeper.

Two — When you bring it up to your doctor, they're going to tell you to take Miralax and drink more water.

And three — There's a reason that advice doesn't work. And a reason nobody's telling you why.

I know this because I've watched it happen from the other side of the exam room.

I've been a nurse for 23 years. I've seen things that would make you lose sleep. But the thing I can't stop thinking about is a 58-year-old woman named Karen who sat on the exam table in our clinic and cried because she hadn't had a bowel movement in eleven days.

Let me tell you what happened to her.

She'd been on Wegovy for five months. Down 31 pounds. Bloodwork was beautiful. A1C improved. Blood pressure down. On paper, she was a textbook success.

I took her vitals and asked the standard questions. She answered everything fine until I asked, "Any digestive issues?"

And she just... stopped talking. Looked at the floor. Then looked at me with this expression I've seen a thousand times — the one where someone is deciding whether to tell the truth or say what they think the doctor wants to hear.

"I haven't gone to the bathroom in eleven days," she said.

I put down my clipboard.

She started talking fast, the way people do when they've been holding something in. The bloating so severe she couldn't button her pants. The sulfur burps that smelled like rotten eggs — so bad her grandson had commented on her breath at his baseball game in front of the whole bleacher section. The pressure in her stomach that kept her up at night. The feeling of food from dinner still sitting there the next morning, like a brick that wouldn't dissolve.

She told me about the enemas. Plural. That she'd given herself one at a gas station bathroom during a road trip because the pain was a ten out of ten and she couldn't make it to her daughter's house.

She told me about her medicine cabinet. Miralax. Dulcolax. Colace. Mag citrate. Fiber gummies. Senna. Smooth Move tea. Prune juice she hid behind the orange juice.

She told me she had a spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she'd gone.

Then she said the thing I hear from every one of these women:

"But I've lost 31 pounds. So I just deal with it."

The medication is giving her the body she's wanted for thirty years. But she's too sick to enjoy living in it.

Sound familiar?

The doctor spent nine minutes with her. I know because I checked.

He told Karen that constipation was a very common side effect. Asked if she was drinking enough water. Suggested increasing her fiber and trying Miralax.

Karen looked at him and said, "I've been taking Miralax every day for three months."

He paused. Typed something into the chart. Said they could try Linzess or consider lowering her dose.

Karen's face went white. "Lower my dose? I've lost thirty-one pounds."

He nodded sympathetically. Follow up in six weeks.

She left. I walked her out. At the door she turned and said, "He didn't hear a single thing I said, did he?"

I wanted to tell her the truth. Instead I said, "Give the Linzess a try and call us if it doesn't help."

She didn't call back. They never do. Because the weight is still coming off. And they've decided the suffering is the price of admission.

But Karen broke something in me. Because she wasn't the first. She was just the one who made me stop handing out the same useless advice and start asking why it never worked.

So I started researching. Not patient forums. Not Facebook groups. The actual studies.

And what I found at 1 AM on my night off, sitting at my kitchen table, made me want to walk back into that exam room and apologize to every woman I'd ever handed a Miralax recommendation to.

Because we were all treating the wrong organ.

Think of digestion as a highway. Food enters at the on-ramp — the stomach. Travels through the middle — the small intestine. Exits at the off-ramp — the colon.

When you hear "constipation," you think colon. Everyone does. That's where things exit. That's where the blockage must be.

But GLP-1 medications don't work at the off-ramp. They slow things down at the on-ramp. The stomach loses its rhythm. Food sits there for hours — sometimes days. It ferments. That's where the sulfur gas comes from. It dries out and hardens. That's the cement feeling.

By the time anything reaches the colon — if it reaches the colon — it's already a brick. The colon isn't blocked. It's empty. The problem was never at the exit.

And every product in Karen's medicine cabinet was aimed at the exit.

Miralax pulls water into the colon to soften what's sitting there. But nothing was sitting there. The blockage was in her stomach, six feet upstream.

Fiber gummies add bulk to help things pass through the colon. When food can't get out of the stomach, adding bulk is packing more cars onto a highway where the on-ramp is closed.

Dulcolax forces the colon to contract. But you can squeeze an empty tube all day long. Nothing comes out if nothing went in.

Smooth Move tea stimulates the lower intestine. Same problem. You can't flush a pipe from the bottom when the clog is at the top.

So the question became: what actually works on the stomach?

I spent three nights on PubMed. Followed citations from paper to paper. Three things kept surfacing.

First — a compound found in high concentrations in celery. Apigenin.

It supports the vagus nerve — the nerve that controls stomach contractions, the nerve that tells the stomach when to push food through. GLP-1 medications essentially mute that signal. Apigenin was showing up in motility studies as a way to gently support it again. Not override the medication. Not force anything. Like turning the volume back up on a speaker someone turned down.

That was the first piece. Get the stomach moving again.

But even with the stomach moving, there's a backlog. Weeks of slow digestion mean bacteria have been producing hydrogen sulfide — sulfur gas — faster than the body can clear it. Getting things moving doesn't fix the gas that's already forming.

The second piece was chlorophyllin — a concentrated form of chlorophyll that binds directly to hydrogen sulfide and neutralizes it before it rises as gas. Doesn't mask the smell. Disarms the molecule that creates it.

Two pieces. But I kept reading. Because even with the stomach moving and the gas handled, everything downstream is backed up too. Weeks of stalled motility mean the small intestine and colon are congested.

The third piece was a specific type of soluble prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber every doctor recommends — that's the last thing a backed-up system needs. This was low-bulk, gel-forming. Draws moisture in. Softens what's stuck without adding volume to the gridlock. Lets things clear once the stomach starts working again.

Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three working together.

That's when I understood why Karen's medicine cabinet never stood a chance. Every product addressed one piece — and most of them addressed the wrong piece entirely.

I started looking for something that combined all three. Found motility supplements with ginger extract but nothing for the gas. Found chlorophyll drops with no motility support. Found fiber blends that would have made everything worse — insoluble bulk on top of an already jammed system.

Everything had one piece. Nothing had all three in the right form.

Then I found a small company I'd never heard of. They'd built a gummy — specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. Not a general digestive supplement repackaged with a new label.

Motilli.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyll. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber. I checked each ingredient against the studies I'd been reading for three nights. Motility support. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three. At concentrations that matched the research.

I ordered two bottles that night. One for me to evaluate. One for Karen.

I called her the next day. She'd stopped coming to our clinic — I wasn't surprised. I told her I'd found something I wanted her to try. Didn't oversell it. Just said it worked on the stomach instead of the colon, and I thought it was worth thirty days.

She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "At this point I'll try anything."

Two gummies a day. She started the following Monday.

Day three she texted: "Nothing yet."

I told her to give it time. This wasn't a laxative. It wasn't forcing anything.

Day five: "Bloating feels a little less. Maybe placebo."

Day ten: "I went this morning. On my own. No Miralax. No enema. Just went."

That text shouldn't have hit as hard as it did.

But it did. Because I knew about the eleven days. The gas station. The spreadsheet. The baseball game.

Week three — the sulfur burps were nearly gone. I thought about her grandson at the baseball game. The whole bleacher section. That didn't have to happen. None of it did.

"I had coffee with my friend Linda this morning," she said. "I didn't think about my breath once. Do you know how long it's been since that happened?"

Month one — she stopped by the clinic. Not as a patient. To see me. She'd thrown out the spreadsheet. Still on Wegovy. Still losing weight. Still had the silence where food didn't run her brain.

But she wasn't paying the tax anymore.

Month two — her husband noticed she was going out again. Saying yes to dinners. Staying for the whole visit at the grandkids' house instead of disappearing every thirty minutes.

"He said I seem like myself again," she told me. "He didn't know I'd been gone."

She went to her grandson's next game. Stayed the whole time.

I've since shared the same research with four other patients. Quietly. On my own time. Every one had the same pattern — weeks of nothing from laxatives, then steady improvement once something was finally working on the stomach instead of the colon.

Here's what I need you to hear — from a nurse who has watched this happen over and over:

Your doctors aren't lying when they say constipation is a common side effect. They're right. But they're wrong about where it starts. And because they're wrong about where it starts, every solution they offer is aimed at the wrong place.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. That's not a mystery. That's mechanics. And until something addresses all three, you can take every laxative in the pharmacy and still end up on day eleven with a spreadsheet and an enema kit in your purse.

You don't have to choose between the weight loss and your digestion. You don't have to accept the tax.

Karen didn't.

And she's back at the baseball games.

He nodded sympathetically. Follow up in six weeks.

Fiber gummies add bulk to help things pass through the colon. When food can't get out of the stomach, adding bulk is packing more cars onto a highway where the on-ramp is closed.

The third piece was a specific type of soluble prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber every doctor recommends — that's the last thing a backed-up system needs. This was low-bulk, gel-forming. Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three working together.

He paused. Typed something into the chart. Said they could try Linzess or consider lowering her dose.

Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

"He said I seem like myself again," she told me. "He didn't know I'd been gone."

She went to her grandson's next game. Stayed the whole time.

She told me she had a spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she'd gone.

Then she said the thing I hear from every one of these women:

"But I've lost 31 pounds. So I just deal with it."

He told Karen that constipation was a very common side effect. Asked if she was drinking enough water. Suggested increasing her fiber and trying Miralax.

Karen looked at him and said, "I've been taking Miralax every day for three months."

He paused. Typed something into the chart. Said they could try Linzess or consider lowering her dose.

Karen's face went white. "Lower my dose? I've lost thirty-one pounds."

He nodded sympathetically. Follow up in six weeks.

She left. I walked her out. At the door she turned and said, "He didn't hear a single thing I said, did he?"

And every product in Karen's medicine cabinet was aimed at the exit.

Miralax pulls water into the colon to soften what's sitting there. But nothing was sitting there. The blockage was in her stomach, six feet upstream.

Fiber gummies add bulk to help things pass through the colon. When food can't get out of the stomach, adding bulk is packing more cars onto a highway where the on-ramp is closed.

Dulcolax forces the colon to contract. But you can squeeze an empty tube all day long. Nothing comes out if nothing went in.

The third piece was a specific type of soluble prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber every doctor recommends — that's the last thing a backed-up system needs. This was low-bulk, gel-forming. Draws moisture in. Softens what's stuck without adding volume to the gridlock. Lets things clear once the stomach starts working again.

Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three working together.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyll. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber. I checked each ingredient against the studies I'd been reading for three nights. Motility support. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three. At concentrations that matched the research.

Month two — her husband noticed she was going out again. Saying yes to dinners. Staying for the whole visit at the grandkids' house instead of disappearing every thirty minutes.

"He said I seem like myself again," she told me. "He didn't know I'd been gone."

She went to her grandson's next game. Stayed the whole time.

She told me she had a spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she'd gone.

Then she said the thing I hear from every one of these women:

He paused. Typed something into the chart. Said they could try Linzess or consider lowering her dose.

He nodded sympathetically. Follow up in six weeks.

First — a compound found in high concentrations in celery. Apigenin.

The third piece was a specific type of soluble prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber every doctor recommends — that's the last thing a backed-up system needs. This was low-bulk, gel-forming. Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three working together.

I started looking for something that combined all three. Found motility supplements with ginger extract but nothing for the gas. Found chlorophyll drops with no motility support. Found fiber blends that would have made everything worse — insoluble bulk on top of an already jammed system.

Everything had one piece. Nothing had all three in the right form.

Motilli.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyll. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber. I checked each ingredient against the studies I'd been reading for three nights. Motility support. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three. At concentrations that matched the research.

I ordered two bottles that night. One for me to evaluate. One for Karen.

I called her the next day. She'd stopped coming to our clinic — I wasn't surprised. I told her I'd found something I wanted her to try. Didn't oversell it. Just said it worked on the stomach instead of the colon, and I thought it was worth thirty days.

She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "At this point I'll try anything."

Two gummies a day. She started the following Monday.

Day three she texted: "Nothing yet."

I told her to give it time. This wasn't a laxative. It wasn't forcing anything.

Day five: "Bloating feels a little less. Maybe placebo."

But she wasn't paying the tax anymore.

Month two — her husband noticed she was going out again. Saying yes to dinners. Staying for the whole visit at the grandkids' house instead of disappearing every thirty minutes.

"He said I seem like myself again," she told me. "He didn't know I'd been gone."

She went to her grandson's next game. Stayed the whole time.

I've since shared the same research with four other patients. Quietly. On my own time. Every one had the same pattern — weeks of nothing from laxatives, then steady improvement once something was finally working on the stomach instead of the colon.

Your doctors aren't lying when they say constipation is a common side effect. They're right. But they're wrong about where it starts. And because they're wrong about where it starts, every solution they offer is aimed at the wrong place.

I put down my clipboard.

She started talking fast, the way people do when they've been holding something in. The bloating so severe she couldn't button her pants. The sulfur burps that smelled like rotten eggs — so bad her grandson had commented on her breath at his baseball game in front of the whole bleacher section. She told me about the enemas. Plural. That she'd given herself one at a gas station bathroom during a road trip because the pain was a ten out of ten and she couldn't make it to her daughter's house.

She told me about her medicine cabinet. Miralax. Dulcolax. Colace. Mag citrate. Fiber gummies. Senna. Smooth Move tea. Prune juice she hid behind the orange juice.

She told me she had a spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she'd gone.

Then she said the thing I hear from every one of these women:

"But I've lost 31 pounds. So I just deal with it."

The medication is giving her the body she's wanted for thirty years. But she's too sick to enjoy living in it.

Sound familiar?

The doctor spent nine minutes with her. I know because I checked.

He told Karen that constipation was a very common side effect. Asked if she was drinking enough water. Suggested increasing her fiber and trying Miralax.

Karen looked at him and said, "I've been taking Miralax every day for three months."

He paused. Typed something into the chart. Said they could try Linzess or consider lowering her dose.

Karen's face went white. "Lower my dose? I've lost thirty-one pounds."

He nodded sympathetically. Follow up in six weeks.

She left. I walked her out. At the door she turned and said, "He didn't hear a single thing I said, did he?"

I wanted to tell her the truth. Instead I said, "Give the Linzess a try and call us if it doesn't help."

But Karen broke something in me. Because she wasn't the first. She was just the one who made me stop handing out the same useless advice and start asking why it never worked.

So I started researching. Not patient forums. Not Facebook groups. The actual studies.

And what I found at 1 AM on my night off, sitting at my kitchen table, made me want to walk back into that exam room and apologize to every woman I'd ever handed a Miralax recommendation to.

Because we were all treating the wrong organ.

Think of digestion as a highway. Food enters at the on-ramp — the stomach. Travels through the middle — the small intestine. Exits at the off-ramp — the colon.

And every product in Karen's medicine cabinet was aimed at the exit.

Miralax pulls water into the colon to soften what's sitting there. But nothing was sitting there. The blockage was in her stomach, six feet upstream.

Fiber gummies add bulk to help things pass through the colon. When food can't get out of the stomach, adding bulk is packing more cars onto a highway where the on-ramp is closed.

Dulcolax forces the colon to contract. But you can squeeze an empty tube all day long. Nothing comes out if nothing went in.

Smooth Move tea stimulates the lower intestine. Same problem. You can't flush a pipe from the bottom when the clog is at the top.

So the question became: what actually works on the stomach?

First — a compound found in high concentrations in celery. Apigenin.

The second piece was chlorophyllin — a concentrated form of chlorophyll that binds directly to hydrogen sulfide and neutralizes it before it rises as gas. Doesn't mask the smell. Disarms the molecule that creates it.

Two pieces. But I kept reading. Because even with the stomach moving and the gas handled, everything downstream is backed up too. Weeks of stalled motility mean the small intestine and colon are congested.

The third piece was a specific type of soluble prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber every doctor recommends — that's the last thing a backed-up system needs. This was low-bulk, gel-forming. Draws moisture in. Softens what's stuck without adding volume to the gridlock. Lets things clear once the stomach starts working again.

Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three working together.

That's when I understood why Karen's medicine cabinet never stood a chance. Every product addressed one piece — and most of them addressed the wrong piece entirely.

I started looking for something that combined all three. Found motility supplements with ginger extract but nothing for the gas. Found chlorophyll drops with no motility support. Found fiber blends that would have made everything worse — insoluble bulk on top of an already jammed system.

Everything had one piece. Nothing had all three in the right form.

Then I found a small company I'd never heard of. They'd built a gummy — specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. Not a general digestive supplement repackaged with a new label.

Motilli.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyll. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber. I checked each ingredient against the studies I'd been reading for three nights. Motility support. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three. At concentrations that matched the research.

I ordered two bottles that night. One for me to evaluate. One for Karen.

I called her the next day. She'd stopped coming to our clinic — I wasn't surprised. I told her I'd found something I wanted her to try. Didn't oversell it. Just said it worked on the stomach instead of the colon, and I thought it was worth thirty days.

She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "At this point I'll try anything."

Two gummies a day. She started the following Monday.

Day three she texted: "Nothing yet."

I told her to give it time. This wasn't a laxative. It wasn't forcing anything.

Day five: "Bloating feels a little less. Maybe placebo."

Day ten: "I went this morning. On my own. No Miralax. No enema. Just went."

But she wasn't paying the tax anymore.

Month two — her husband noticed she was going out again. Saying yes to dinners. Staying for the whole visit at the grandkids' house instead of disappearing every thirty minutes.

"He said I seem like myself again," she told me. "He didn't know I'd been gone."

She went to her grandson's next game. Stayed the whole time.

I've since shared the same research with four other patients. Quietly. On my own time. Every one had the same pattern — weeks of nothing from laxatives, then steady improvement once something was finally working on the stomach instead of the colon.

Here's what I need you to hear — from a nurse who has watched this happen over and over:

Your doctors aren't lying when they say constipation is a common side effect. They're right. But they're wrong about where it starts. And because they're wrong about where it starts, every solution they offer is aimed at the wrong place.

You don't have to choose between the weight loss and your digestion. You don't have to accept the tax.

Karen didn't.

She told me about her medicine cabinet. Miralax. Dulcolax. Colace. Mag citrate. Fiber gummies. Senna. Smooth Move tea. Prune juice she hid behind the orange juice.

She told me she had a spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she'd gone.

Then she said the thing I hear from every one of these women:

"But I've lost 31 pounds. So I just deal with it."

Sound familiar?

He told Karen that constipation was a very common side effect. Asked if she was drinking enough water. Suggested increasing her fiber and trying Miralax.

He paused. Typed something into the chart. Said they could try Linzess or consider lowering her dose.

Karen's face went white. "Lower my dose? I've lost thirty-one pounds."

He nodded sympathetically. Follow up in six weeks.

But Karen broke something in me. Because she wasn't the first. She was just the one who made me stop handing out the same useless advice and start asking why it never worked.

So I started researching. Not patient forums. Not Facebook groups. The actual studies.

And what I found at 1 AM on my night off, sitting at my kitchen table, made me want to walk back into that exam room and apologize to every woman I'd ever handed a Miralax recommendation to.

Because we were all treating the wrong organ.

Think of digestion as a highway. Food enters at the on-ramp — the stomach. Travels through the middle — the small intestine. Exits at the off-ramp — the colon.

So the question became: what actually works on the stomach?

I spent three nights on PubMed. Followed citations from paper to paper. Three things kept surfacing.

First — a compound found in high concentrations in celery. Apigenin.

The third piece was a specific type of soluble prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber every doctor recommends — that's the last thing a backed-up system needs. This was low-bulk, gel-forming. Draws moisture in. Softens what's stuck without adding volume to the gridlock. Lets things clear once the stomach starts working again.

Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three working together.

That's when I understood why Karen's medicine cabinet never stood a chance. Every product addressed one piece — and most of them addressed the wrong piece entirely.

I started looking for something that combined all three. Found motility supplements with ginger extract but nothing for the gas. Found chlorophyll drops with no motility support. Found fiber blends that would have made everything worse — insoluble bulk on top of an already jammed system.

Everything had one piece. Nothing had all three in the right form.

Then I found a small company I'd never heard of. They'd built a gummy — specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. Not a general digestive supplement repackaged with a new label.

Motilli.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyll. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber. I checked each ingredient against the studies I'd been reading for three nights. Motility support. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three. At concentrations that matched the research.

I ordered two bottles that night. One for me to evaluate. One for Karen.

I called her the next day. She'd stopped coming to our clinic — I wasn't surprised. I told her I'd found something I wanted her to try. Didn't oversell it. Just said it worked on the stomach instead of the colon, and I thought it was worth thirty days.

She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "At this point I'll try anything."

Two gummies a day. She started the following Monday.

Day three she texted: "Nothing yet."

I told her to give it time. This wasn't a laxative. It wasn't forcing anything.

Day five: "Bloating feels a little less. Maybe placebo."

Day ten: "I went this morning. On my own. No Miralax. No enema. Just went."

That text shouldn't have hit as hard as it did.

But it did. Because I knew about the eleven days. The gas station. The spreadsheet. The baseball game.

Week three — the sulfur burps were nearly gone. I thought about her grandson at the baseball game. The whole bleacher section. That didn't have to happen. None of it did.

"I had coffee with my friend Linda this morning," she said. "I didn't think about my breath once. Do you know how long it's been since that happened?"

Month one — she stopped by the clinic. Not as a patient. To see me. She'd thrown out the spreadsheet. Still on Wegovy. Still losing weight. Still had the silence where food didn't run her brain.

But she wasn't paying the tax anymore.

Month two — her husband noticed she was going out again. Saying yes to dinners. Staying for the whole visit at the grandkids' house instead of disappearing every thirty minutes.

"He said I seem like myself again," she told me. "He didn't know I'd been gone."

She went to her grandson's next game. Stayed the whole time.

I've since shared the same research with four other patients. Quietly. On my own time. Every one had the same pattern — weeks of nothing from laxatives, then steady improvement once something was finally working on the stomach instead of the colon.

Here's what I need you to hear — from a nurse who has watched this happen over and over:

Your doctors aren't lying when they say constipation is a common side effect. They're right. But they're wrong about where it starts. And because they're wrong about where it starts, every solution they offer is aimed at the wrong place.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. That's not a mystery. That's mechanics. And until something addresses all three, you can take every laxative in the pharmacy and still end up on day eleven with a spreadsheet and an enema kit in your purse.

You don't have to choose between the weight loss and your digestion. You don't have to accept the tax.

Karen didn't.

And she's back at the baseball games.

Here's what's happening right now:

One — The medication that's finally silencing your food noise is quietly wrecking your digestion from the top down. Not just "causing constipation." Something deeper.

Two — When you bring it up to your doctor, they're going to tell you to take Miralax and drink more water.

And three — There's a reason that advice doesn't work. And a reason nobody's telling you why.

I know this because I've watched it happen from the other side of the exam room.

I've been a nurse for 23 years. I've seen things that would make you lose sleep. But the thing I can't stop thinking about is a 58-year-old woman named Karen who sat on the exam table in our clinic and cried because she hadn't had a bowel movement in eleven days.

Let me tell you what happened to her.

She'd been on Wegovy for five months. Down 31 pounds. Bloodwork was beautiful. A1C improved. Blood pressure down. On paper, she was a textbook success.

I took her vitals and asked the standard questions. She answered everything fine until I asked, "Any digestive issues?"

And she just... stopped talking. Looked at the floor. Then looked at me with this expression I've seen a thousand times — the one where someone is deciding whether to tell the truth or say what they think the doctor wants to hear.

"I haven't gone to the bathroom in eleven days," she said.

I put down my clipboard.

She started talking fast, the way people do when they've been holding something in. The bloating so severe she couldn't button her pants. The sulfur burps that smelled like rotten eggs — so bad her grandson had commented on her breath at his baseball game in front of the whole bleacher section. The pressure in her stomach that kept her up at night. The feeling of food from dinner still sitting there the next morning, like a brick that wouldn't dissolve.

She told me about the enemas. Plural. That she'd given herself one at a gas station bathroom during a road trip because the pain was a ten out of ten and she couldn't make it to her daughter's house.

She told me about her medicine cabinet. Miralax. Dulcolax. Colace. Mag citrate. Fiber gummies. Senna. Smooth Move tea. Prune juice she hid behind the orange juice.

She told me she had a spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she'd gone.

Then she said the thing I hear from every one of these women:

"But I've lost 31 pounds. So I just deal with it."

The medication is giving her the body she's wanted for thirty years. But she's too sick to enjoy living in it.

Sound familiar?

The doctor spent nine minutes with her. I know because I checked.

He told Karen that constipation was a very common side effect. Asked if she was drinking enough water. Suggested increasing her fiber and trying Miralax.

Karen looked at him and said, "I've been taking Miralax every day for three months."

He paused. Typed something into the chart. Said they could try Linzess or consider lowering her dose.

Karen's face went white. "Lower my dose? I've lost thirty-one pounds."

He nodded sympathetically. Follow up in six weeks.

She left. I walked her out. At the door she turned and said, "He didn't hear a single thing I said, did he?"

I wanted to tell her the truth. Instead I said, "Give the Linzess a try and call us if it doesn't help."

She didn't call back. They never do. Because the weight is still coming off. And they've decided the suffering is the price of admission.

But Karen broke something in me. Because she wasn't the first. She was just the one who made me stop handing out the same useless advice and start asking why it never worked.

So I started researching. Not patient forums. Not Facebook groups. The actual studies.

And what I found at 1 AM on my night off, sitting at my kitchen table, made me want to walk back into that exam room and apologize to every woman I'd ever handed a Miralax recommendation to.

Because we were all treating the wrong organ.

Think of digestion as a highway. Food enters at the on-ramp — the stomach. Travels through the middle — the small intestine. Exits at the off-ramp — the colon.

When you hear "constipation," you think colon. Everyone does. That's where things exit. That's where the blockage must be.

But GLP-1 medications don't work at the off-ramp. They slow things down at the on-ramp. The stomach loses its rhythm. Food sits there for hours — sometimes days. It ferments. That's where the sulfur gas comes from. It dries out and hardens. That's the cement feeling.

By the time anything reaches the colon — if it reaches the colon — it's already a brick. The colon isn't blocked. It's empty. The problem was never at the exit.

And every product in Karen's medicine cabinet was aimed at the exit.

Miralax pulls water into the colon to soften what's sitting there. But nothing was sitting there. The blockage was in her stomach, six feet upstream.

Fiber gummies add bulk to help things pass through the colon. When food can't get out of the stomach, adding bulk is packing more cars onto a highway where the on-ramp is closed.

Dulcolax forces the colon to contract. But you can squeeze an empty tube all day long. Nothing comes out if nothing went in.

Smooth Move tea stimulates the lower intestine. Same problem. You can't flush a pipe from the bottom when the clog is at the top.

So the question became: what actually works on the stomach?

I spent three nights on PubMed. Followed citations from paper to paper. Three things kept surfacing.

First — a compound found in high concentrations in celery. Apigenin.

It supports the vagus nerve — the nerve that controls stomach contractions, the nerve that tells the stomach when to push food through. GLP-1 medications essentially mute that signal. Apigenin was showing up in motility studies as a way to gently support it again. Not override the medication. Not force anything. Like turning the volume back up on a speaker someone turned down.

That was the first piece. Get the stomach moving again.

But even with the stomach moving, there's a backlog. Weeks of slow digestion mean bacteria have been producing hydrogen sulfide — sulfur gas — faster than the body can clear it. Getting things moving doesn't fix the gas that's already forming.

The second piece was chlorophyllin — a concentrated form of chlorophyll that binds directly to hydrogen sulfide and neutralizes it before it rises as gas. Doesn't mask the smell. Disarms the molecule that creates it.

Two pieces. But I kept reading. Because even with the stomach moving and the gas handled, everything downstream is backed up too. Weeks of stalled motility mean the small intestine and colon are congested.

The third piece was a specific type of soluble prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber every doctor recommends — that's the last thing a backed-up system needs. This was low-bulk, gel-forming. Draws moisture in. Softens what's stuck without adding volume to the gridlock. Lets things clear once the stomach starts working again.

Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three working together.

That's when I understood why Karen's medicine cabinet never stood a chance. Every product addressed one piece — and most of them addressed the wrong piece entirely.

I started looking for something that combined all three. Found motility supplements with ginger extract but nothing for the gas. Found chlorophyll drops with no motility support. Found fiber blends that would have made everything worse — insoluble bulk on top of an already jammed system.

Everything had one piece. Nothing had all three in the right form.

Then I found a small company I'd never heard of. They'd built a gummy — specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. Not a general digestive supplement repackaged with a new label.

Motilli.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyll. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber. I checked each ingredient against the studies I'd been reading for three nights. Motility support. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three. At concentrations that matched the research.

I ordered two bottles that night. One for me to evaluate. One for Karen.

I called her the next day. She'd stopped coming to our clinic — I wasn't surprised. I told her I'd found something I wanted her to try. Didn't oversell it. Just said it worked on the stomach instead of the colon, and I thought it was worth thirty days.

She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "At this point I'll try anything."

Two gummies a day. She started the following Monday.

Day three she texted: "Nothing yet."

I told her to give it time. This wasn't a laxative. It wasn't forcing anything.

Day five: "Bloating feels a little less. Maybe placebo."

Day ten: "I went this morning. On my own. No Miralax. No enema. Just went."

That text shouldn't have hit as hard as it did.

But it did. Because I knew about the eleven days. The gas station. The spreadsheet. The baseball game.

Week three — the sulfur burps were nearly gone. I thought about her grandson at the baseball game. The whole bleacher section. That didn't have to happen. None of it did.

"I had coffee with my friend Linda this morning," she said. "I didn't think about my breath once. Do you know how long it's been since that happened?"

Month one — she stopped by the clinic. Not as a patient. To see me. She'd thrown out the spreadsheet. Still on Wegovy. Still losing weight. Still had the silence where food didn't run her brain.

But she wasn't paying the tax anymore.

Month two — her husband noticed she was going out again. Saying yes to dinners. Staying for the whole visit at the grandkids' house instead of disappearing every thirty minutes.

"He said I seem like myself again," she told me. "He didn't know I'd been gone."

She went to her grandson's next game. Stayed the whole time.

I've since shared the same research with four other patients. Quietly. On my own time. Every one had the same pattern — weeks of nothing from laxatives, then steady improvement once something was finally working on the stomach instead of the colon.

Here's what I need you to hear — from a nurse who has watched this happen over and over:

Your doctors aren't lying when they say constipation is a common side effect. They're right. But they're wrong about where it starts. And because they're wrong about where it starts, every solution they offer is aimed at the wrong place.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. That's not a mystery. That's mechanics. And until something addresses all three, you can take every laxative in the pharmacy and still end up on day eleven with a spreadsheet and an enema kit in your purse.

You don't have to choose between the weight loss and your digestion. You don't have to accept the tax.

Karen didn't.

And she's back at the baseball games.

creative.body:
If you're on Ozempic, Wegovy, or Mounjaro and your stomach feels like it's full of cement, you can't stop burping sulfur, and you haven't had a normal bowel movement in weeks, I need you to hear this.

Because what I'm about to tell you is going to make you furious.

Here's what's happening right now:

One — The medication that's finally silencing your food noise is quietly wrecking your digestion from the top down. Not just "causing constipation." Something deeper.

Two — When you bring it up to your doctor, they're going to tell you to take Miralax and drink more water.

And three — There's a reason that advice doesn't work. And a reason nobody's telling you why.

I know this because I've watched it happen from the other side of the exam room.

I've been a nurse for 23 years. I've seen things that would make you lose sleep. But the thing I can't stop thinking about is a 58-year-old woman named Karen who sat on the exam table in our clinic and cried because she hadn't had a bowel movement in eleven days.

Let me tell you what happened to her.

She'd been on Wegovy for five months. Down 31 pounds. Bloodwork was beautiful. A1C improved. Blood pressure down. On paper, she was a textbook success.

I took her vitals and asked the standard questions. She answered everything fine until I asked, "Any digestive issues?"

And she just... stopped talking. Looked at the floor. Then looked at me with this expression I've seen a thousand times — the one where someone is deciding whether to tell the truth or say what they think the doctor wants to hear.

"I haven't gone to the bathroom in eleven days," she said.

I put down my clipboard.

She started talking fast, the way people do when they've been holding something in. The bloating so severe she couldn't button her pants. The sulfur burps that smelled like rotten eggs — so bad her grandson had commented on her breath at his baseball game in front of the whole bleacher section. The pressure in her stomach that kept her up at night. The feeling of food from dinner still sitting there the next morning, like a brick that wouldn't dissolve.

She told me about the enemas. Plural. That she'd given herself one at a gas station bathroom during a road trip because the pain was a ten out of ten and she couldn't make it to her daughter's house.

She told me about her medicine cabinet. Miralax. Dulcolax. Colace. Mag citrate. Fiber gummies. Senna. Smooth Move tea. Prune juice she hid behind the orange juice.

She told me she had a spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she'd gone.

Then she said the thing I hear from every one of these women:

"But I've lost 31 pounds. So I just deal with it."

The medication is giving her the body she's wanted for thirty years. But she's too sick to enjoy living in it.

Sound familiar?

The doctor spent nine minutes with her. I know because I checked.

He told Karen that constipation was a very common side effect. Asked if she was drinking enough water. Suggested increasing her fiber and trying Miralax.

Karen looked at him and said, "I've been taking Miralax every day for three months."

He paused. Typed something into the chart. Said they could try Linzess or consider lowering her dose.

Karen's face went white. "Lower my dose? I've lost thirty-one pounds."

He nodded sympathetically. Follow up in six weeks.

She left. I walked her out. At the door she turned and said, "He didn't hear a single thing I said, did he?"

I wanted to tell her the truth. Instead I said, "Give the Linzess a try and call us if it doesn't help."

She didn't call back. They never do. Because the weight is still coming off. And they've decided the suffering is the price of admission.

But Karen broke something in me. Because she wasn't the first. She was just the one who made me stop handing out the same useless advice and start asking why it never worked.

So I started researching. Not patient forums. Not Facebook groups. The actual studies.

And what I found at 1 AM on my night off, sitting at my kitchen table, made me want to walk back into that exam room and apologize to every woman I'd ever handed a Miralax recommendation to.

Because we were all treating the wrong organ.

Think of digestion as a highway. Food enters at the on-ramp — the stomach. Travels through the middle — the small intestine. Exits at the off-ramp — the colon.

When you hear "constipation," you think colon. Everyone does. That's where things exit. That's where the blockage must be.

But GLP-1 medications don't work at the off-ramp. They slow things down at the on-ramp. The stomach loses its rhythm. Food sits there for hours — sometimes days. It ferments. That's where the sulfur gas comes from. It dries out and hardens. That's the cement feeling.

By the time anything reaches the colon — if it reaches the colon — it's already a brick. The colon isn't blocked. It's empty. The problem was never at the exit.

And every product in Karen's medicine cabinet was aimed at the exit.

Miralax pulls water into the colon to soften what's sitting there. But nothing was sitting there. The blockage was in her stomach, six feet upstream.

Fiber gummies add bulk to help things pass through the colon. When food can't get out of the stomach, adding bulk is packing more cars onto a highway where the on-ramp is closed.

Dulcolax forces the colon to contract. But you can squeeze an empty tube all day long. Nothing comes out if nothing went in.

Smooth Move tea stimulates the lower intestine. Same problem. You can't flush a pipe from the bottom when the clog is at the top.

So the question became: what actually works on the stomach?

I spent three nights on PubMed. Followed citations from paper to paper. Three things kept surfacing.

First — a compound found in high concentrations in celery. Apigenin.

It supports the vagus nerve — the nerve that controls stomach contractions, the nerve that tells the stomach when to push food through. GLP-1 medications essentially mute that signal. Apigenin was showing up in motility studies as a way to gently support it again. Not override the medication. Not force anything. Like turning the volume back up on a speaker someone turned down.

That was the first piece. Get the stomach moving again.

But even with the stomach moving, there's a backlog. Weeks of slow digestion mean bacteria have been producing hydrogen sulfide — sulfur gas — faster than the body can clear it. Getting things moving doesn't fix the gas that's already forming.

The second piece was chlorophyllin — a concentrated form of chlorophyll that binds directly to hydrogen sulfide and neutralizes it before it rises as gas. Doesn't mask the smell. Disarms the molecule that creates it.

Two pieces. But I kept reading. Because even with the stomach moving and the gas handled, everything downstream is backed up too. Weeks of stalled motility mean the small intestine and colon are congested.

The third piece was a specific type of soluble prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber every doctor recommends — that's the last thing a backed-up system needs. This was low-bulk, gel-forming. Draws moisture in. Softens what's stuck without adding volume to the gridlock. Lets things clear once the stomach starts working again.

Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three working together.

That's when I understood why Karen's medicine cabinet never stood a chance. Every product addressed one piece — and most of them addressed the wrong piece entirely.

I started looking for something that combined all three. Found motility supplements with ginger extract but nothing for the gas. Found chlorophyll drops with no motility support. Found fiber blends that would have made everything worse — insoluble bulk on top of an already jammed system.

Everything had one piece. Nothing had all three in the right form.

Then I found a small company I'd never heard of. They'd built a gummy — specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. Not a general digestive supplement repackaged with a new label.

Motilli.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyll. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber. I checked each ingredient against the studies I'd been reading for three nights. Motility support. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three. At concentrations that matched the research.

I ordered two bottles that night. One for me to evaluate. One for Karen.

I called her the next day. She'd stopped coming to our clinic — I wasn't surprised. I told her I'd found something I wanted her to try. Didn't oversell it. Just said it worked on the stomach instead of the colon, and I thought it was worth thirty days.

She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "At this point I'll try anything."

Two gummies a day. She started the following Monday.

Day three she texted: "Nothing yet."

I told her to give it time. This wasn't a laxative. It wasn't forcing anything.

Day five: "Bloating feels a little less. Maybe placebo."

Day ten: "I went this morning. On my own. No Miralax. No enema. Just went."

That text shouldn't have hit as hard as it did.

But it did. Because I knew about the eleven days. The gas station. The spreadsheet. The baseball game.

Week three — the sulfur burps were nearly gone. I thought about her grandson at the baseball game. The whole bleacher section. That didn't have to happen. None of it did.

"I had coffee with my friend Linda this morning," she said. "I didn't think about my breath once. Do you know how long it's been since that happened?"

Month one — she stopped by the clinic. Not as a patient. To see me. She'd thrown out the spreadsheet. Still on Wegovy. Still losing weight. Still had the silence where food didn't run her brain.

But she wasn't paying the tax anymore.

Month two — her husband noticed she was going out again. Saying yes to dinners. Staying for the whole visit at the grandkids' house instead of disappearing every thirty minutes.

"He said I seem like myself again," she told me. "He didn't know I'd been gone."

She went to her grandson's next game. Stayed the whole time.

I've since shared the same research with four other patients. Quietly. On my own time. Every one had the same pattern — weeks of nothing from laxatives, then steady improvement once something was finally working on the stomach instead of the colon.

Here's what I need you to hear — from a nurse who has watched this happen over and over:

Your doctors aren't lying when they say constipation is a common side effect. They're right. But they're wrong about where it starts. And because they're wrong about where it starts, every solution they offer is aimed at the wrong place.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. That's not a mystery. That's mechanics. And until something addresses all three, you can take every laxative in the pharmacy and still end up on day eleven with a spreadsheet and an enema kit in your purse.

You don't have to choose between the weight loss and your digestion. You don't have to accept the tax.

Karen didn't.

And she's back at the baseball games.

My husband stopped kissing me the month I lost 26 pounds.

Not all at once. He just started aiming for my forehead instead of my mouth. And I let him. Because I knew what he'd find if he got any closer.

Three months on Mounjaro. Down 26 pounds. Two pant sizes gone. My doctor kept saying "incredible."

And I was rotting from the inside out.

Around week five, the burps started. Not normal burps. These tasted like something had crawled inside me and died. Sulfur — hot, thick, completely unpredictable. Mid-conversation at dinner. Mid-kiss goodnight. It would just come, and there was nothing I could do except swallow it back down and pray nobody noticed.

I'd never had a stomach problem in 46 years. Not once. My gut was the one part of my body I never thought about. Six weeks into Mounjaro, I woke up at 2am with acid crawling up my throat so bad I drove to Walgreens in my pajamas and bought Tums for the first time in my life.

I started chewing gum constantly. Mints in every pocket, every purse, my car. I'd excuse myself mid-conversation just to let one out in private, then come back smiling like nothing happened.

Greg never said a word. That was worse. It wasn't a fight. It was his hand not reaching for mine on the couch. The forehead kiss replacing the real one — and both of us pretending that was normal.

My thirteen-year-old walked in one night while I was rinsing my mouth at the sink. "Mom, are you okay? Your breath smells weird." I told her I ate something bad. I was lying to my daughter about my own body.

I stopped accepting dinner invitations. Started eating alone in the kitchen after everyone finished — window open, praying nothing came up while my kids were still in the house.

That's the trade nobody warns you about. They show you the before-and-after photos. They don't show you the woman eating alone because she can't sit at the table with people she loves.

One night I sat on the edge of the bathtub and made myself be honest.

Option one: stay on Mounjaro. Keep losing weight. Keep the mints, the lies, the forehead kisses.

Option two: quit. Watch the 26 pounds come back.

Disappear physically or disappear from the people around me. Either way, I lose.

I refuse to believe those are the only two doors.

My sister-in-law Rachel is a pharmacist — the kind who reads every drug monograph and stays current on research. She's who our family calls before anyone takes anything. I called her on a Tuesday night, close to tears.

She wasn't even surprised.

What she told me made me furious. Not at her. At everything I'd been doing for the past three months.

GLP-1 medications slow down gastric emptying. That's the whole point — that's how they suppress appetite.

But when food sits in your stomach longer than your body is designed for, bacteria go to work on it. They ferment it. Like a traffic jam that turns into a junkyard.

That fermentation produces hydrogen sulfide gas.

That's the sulfur. That's the rotten egg taste. That's what I'd been tasting at the back of my throat for three months.

And the pressure from food sitting too long pushes stomach acid up into your esophagus.

That's the reflux. That's why I suddenly had heartburn at 46 after a lifetime of nothing.

One problem — food not moving. Two symptoms — sulfur and acid. Cause and effect.

And here's the part that made me angry.

The things I'd been buying at the drugstore — Gas-X, Tums, Pepcid, Pepto — none of them touch motility. Not one. Gas-X breaks up air bubbles, but my problem wasn't trapped air — it was fermentation gas being produced continuously. Like running a fan in a room where the fire's still burning. Tums and Pepcid managed the acid but didn't touch the pressure pushing it up. Pepto actually helped the sulfur — but my doctor said I couldn't take it long-term.

Four products. All working downstream. None of them going where the problem actually starts.

I'd spent three months treating symptoms of a problem I didn't understand. Three months closer to quitting the medication entirely.

Rachel said three things actually matter for what GLP-1s do to the gut.

First — something that supports motility. Something that helps wake up your stomach and nudge food forward instead of letting it sit. She said celery juice contains compounds that work with the muscles in your digestive tract. Not a laxative. A gentle nudge to get things moving again.

Second — something that neutralizes the sulfur compounds from the inside. Not masking the smell like mints do. Going after the hydrogen sulfide gas itself. Chlorophyll — a natural internal deodorizer that breaks down sulfide compounds at the source.

Third — the right kind of fiber. When digestion is this slow, the wrong fiber sits on top of everything and adds to the bloating. But gentle, soluble fiber helps things move through without making the jam worse.

All three working together. Motility. Neutralization. Flow. Take away any one and the cycle starts right back up.

I spent two nights after the kids went to bed going through ingredient lists like I was studying for a final. Every product had one piece. Maybe two. Nothing combined all three.

I was about to close my laptop when I found a small company called Motilli. Celery juice-based gummy made specifically for people on GLP-1 medications.

I opened the ingredient panel and went through it line by line.

Celery juice for motility. Chlorophyll for gas neutralization. The right fiber for flow.

All three. In one gummy. The first product I'd found in two nights of searching that actually matched what Rachel described.

I ordered a bottle. My next injection was in four days. If this didn't work, I was calling my prescriber the following Monday and telling her I was done.

The package arrived on a Thursday.

I opened the bottle. Chewed two gummies that morning before breakfast. They tasted like green apple. I put the bottle next to the coffee maker where I'd see it every day and told myself not to expect anything.

I'd been disappointed too many times.

Nothing the first two days. Nothing on day three.

Day four — the burps after lunch were softer. The sulfur edge was fading. Not gone. But fading. More like a normal burp than that hot, rotten wave I'd been bracing for every time I opened my mouth.

By the end of week two, I went an entire Saturday without a single one. I didn't realize it until brushing my teeth that night — I hadn't thought about my breath once all day. I'd eaten lunch at the kitchen table with my family. Not alone by the window. At the table.

Week three I started sleeping through the night. By week five, I stopped buying Tums entirely. At my eight-week check-in, my doctor pulled up the ingredient profile and said, "This actually makes sense for what these medications do."

But here's the moment I keep coming back to.

About six weeks in. Greg and I were watching TV. A Tuesday. He leaned over and kissed me. Not on the forehead. On the mouth. Like it was nothing. Like it was just what you do when you're sitting next to someone you love.

He didn't hold his breath. He didn't pull away. He just kissed me and went back to the show.

I went to the bathroom and cried. Not because anything dramatic happened. Because something normal happened. And I'd forgotten what normal felt like.

I told my friend Dana — same sulfur problem on Wegovy for months. She ordered that night. Called me eleven days later: "I just had dinner at a restaurant with my boyfriend for the first time since March."

My mom started Zepbound and I sent her a bottle. Two weeks later she texted: "Order me three more. I'm not running out of these."

My cousin Allie had quit Mounjaro entirely because of the burps. Gained back 19 pounds. She went back on with the gummies from day one. Five weeks in — down 11 pounds, zero sulfur burps. "I didn't know you could do this medication without the suffering part."

I'm still on Mounjaro. Still losing weight. And I'm no longer paying for it with my marriage, my confidence, or my ability to sit in a room without an exit plan.

If you know what sulfur tastes like at the back of your throat — if you've been declining invitations, eating alone, lying about your breath — hear this.

You are not someone who has to choose between the weight loss and the people you love. That's a false binary. Every solution you've tried failed because they were built for a different problem.

Your family doesn't need you smaller. They need you present. Sitting at the table. Kissing them goodnight without doing math about how close is too close.

Every week you spend managing this with band-aids that don't reach the real problem is another week pulling away from the people who want you near them. That's not discipline. That's not "pushing through." That's accepting a trade you were never required to make.

Motilli gave me back the version of myself that could sit close to people without calculating the risk. I think it could do the same for you.

If you've taken Ozempic or Wegovy and felt like your stomach turned into a concrete mixer, I need you to know something.

What you're calling "constipation" probably isn't constipation.

I didn't understand that until six weeks ago.

I remember the exact moment it clicked.

I was in my bathroom, on day five of not going, crying into a towel so my husband wouldn't hear me.

I had taken Miralax the night before. Nothing.

I had eaten prunes. Nothing.

I had tried Mag07, fiber gummies, Smooth Move tea — the whole rotation.

Nothing.

And I remember thinking: Why won't my body just WORK?

I had been on Wegovy for four months at that point. Lost 27 pounds. Best thing that ever happened to me. For the first time in 30 years, the "food noise" was silent. I wasn't thinking about what I'd eat next or calculating calories in my head while I watched TV.

I was finally free.

Except I wasn't.

Because while the weight was coming off, something else was happening. My digestion had just... stopped.

Not slowed down. Stopped.

I'd eat dinner at 6 PM and still feel it sitting there the next morning. Like a brick. Like wet cement. I would burp — these horrible, rotten-egg sulfur burps — and want to crawl into a hole.

I started avoiding restaurants. Avoiding friends. I made excuses to skip my niece's birthday party because I couldn't trust my own body.

Then I stopped answering the phone.

My sister called three times the week before Thanksgiving and I let it ring every time because the last time we talked, mid-sentence, I felt one of those burps rising and had to pretend I was coughing. The silence on her end told me she smelled it. Or heard it. Or both. I hung up and didn't call back for two days.

I was finally skinny enough to wear a dress again, but I was too sick to leave the house.

That's the part nobody talks about. Everyone sees the weight loss. Everyone says "You look amazing!" And you smile and say thank you while your stomach is a clenched fist of rotting food and you're doing math in your head about whether the nearest bathroom has a fan.

I started to wonder if this was just the deal. Thin but miserable. Smaller but sicker. Like there was a tax on feeling good about how I looked, and the payment was everything else — dinners with friends, weekend trips, sleeping through the night.

One night I sat on the edge of the tub at 2 AM and thought: Is this worth it?

And the honest answer — the one that scared me — was that I didn't know anymore.

So I did what everyone does. I googled.

"Constipation on Ozempic help." "Why won't Miralax work." "GLP-1 stomach problems."

Every forum, every Reddit thread, every Facebook group — same advice. Take more fiber. Drink more water. Try a stronger laxative.

I tried ALL of it.

Do you know what it's like to drink an entire bottle of Miralax over a weekend and not go? To wake up MORE bloated than before?

It felt like my body was broken in a way nothing could fix.

Then my cousin — she's a GI specialist — sent me a voice message.

"Honey, I need you to hear something. What you're experiencing isn't regular constipation. And that's why nothing you're trying is working. You don't have one problem. You have three. And everything you've been taking only touches one of them — badly."

She told me to call her when I had twenty minutes. I called her that night.

"First," she said, "let's talk about why nothing is moving. Imagine your digestion as a conveyor belt. Food goes in at the top — your stomach. Moves through the middle — small intestine. Exits at the end — the colon. Laxatives work on the exit. They push the door open at the END of the line. But GLP-1s like Ozempic and Wegovy work at the BEGINNING. They slow the belt at the START. That's why you feel full after three bites."

She paused.

"But here's what nobody tells you. In some people, the conveyor belt doesn't just slow down. It STOPS. Your stomach muscles fall asleep. Doctors call it gastroparesis — stomach paralysis. The food just sits there."

I told her that's exactly what it felt like.

"Right. So then you try a laxative. But the laxative is yelling at the exit door: OPEN UP! Meanwhile, nothing has moved past the entrance. It's like trying to empty a bathtub by unplugging the drain when the faucet is jammed. That's Problem Number One. Your stomach muscles are asleep. Every laxative you've tried works downstream. Your problem is upstream."

"Okay," I said. "So what about the burps? The sulfur?"

"That's Problem Number Two," she said. "And it's directly connected. When food sits in your stomach too long, it doesn't just sit there politely. It ferments. The bacteria in your gut start breaking it down before your stomach can move it along, and that fermentation produces hydrogen sulfide gas. That's the rotten-egg smell. That's the taste you get in the back of your throat. That's what's clearing the room when you burp."

She explained that no laxative addresses that. Laxatives don't touch gas. They don't neutralize sulfur. They work on stool in the colon — they have nothing to say about fermentation happening in the stomach. So even if a laxative eventually helped things move, the sulfur would still be there. The burps would still be there.

"And Problem Number Three," she said, "is that the fiber you've been taking is making everything worse."

That one hit me. I had a cabinet full of fiber supplements. Metamucil. Psyllium husk capsules. Fiber gummies from three different brands.

"There are two kinds of fiber," she said. "Insoluble fiber — the psyllium, the Metamucil, the bran — works by adding bulk. Makes the stool bigger so your colon has something to push against. In a normal digestive system, that's fine. But your stomach can't empty. So when you add bulk fiber to a stomach that's paralyzed, you're stuffing more luggage into a car that won't start. That's why you felt MORE bloated after taking Miralax. That's why the fiber gummies made it worse. You were adding volume to a system that couldn't handle the volume it already had."

I sat there staring at the wall. Four months of suffering. Hundreds of dollars on supplements. And every single thing I'd tried was either aimed at the wrong part of my body, ignoring the gas entirely, or actively making the blockage worse.

Three problems. Not one.

"So what do I do?" I asked. "How do you fix three things at once?"

"You address each one separately," she said. "And then you need all three working together."

"For Problem One — the paralyzed stomach — you need something that actually wakes up the muscles. There are certain natural compounds found in celery juice, of all places, that support the nerve controlling stomach movement. The vagus nerve. The same nerve that GLP-1s basically put to sleep. The compound is called apigenin, and it's one of the few things that works upstream, right where your problem is. Think of it like physical therapy for your gut. You're not forcing anything. You're teaching the muscle to move again."

"For Problem Two — the sulfur — you need something that neutralizes the gas itself while the motility catches up. Chlorophyll does that. It works like an internal deodorant — it doesn't mask the smell, it binds to the sulfur compounds that create it. It goes after the hydrogen sulfide directly."

"And for Problem Three — you do need fiber to help things move once your stomach starts working again. But not the kind you've been taking. You need a gentle soluble fiber. The kind that softens things by drawing in moisture instead of adding bulk. It dissolves. It doesn't expand. It helps the stool pass without making the blockage bigger."

I wrote all three down on the back of a grocery receipt. Apigenin. Chlorophyll. Soluble fiber. Three things working on three different parts of the problem.

"So I just — what?" I said. "Buy celery juice and chlorophyll drops and some kind of fiber powder and take them all separately?"

She paused. "You could try. But honestly, the celery juice is the hard part. You'd need about sixteen ounces a day to get enough apigenin. And right now you can barely keep down a few bites of toast. That volume of liquid would make everything worse."

She was right. I had tried juicing last year. The smell alone made me gag. And the amount of liquid made me feel like I was drowning from the inside.

"I'd look into whether anyone's combined them," she said. "I know the research on the individual compounds. I don't keep up with the supplement side."

That was the end of our conversation. She gave me the map. She didn't give me the destination.

So I went looking.

I spent three nights on my laptop after my husband went to bed, searching for anything that combined those three things. Most of what I found was one or the other — celery juice powders with nothing else, chlorophyll drops meant for skin, fiber supplements that were just more of the same bulk I'd already tried.

Then I found a gummy. A concentrated celery juice gummy that had all three — the apigenin, the chlorophyll, and a gentle soluble fiber — in a form that didn't require drinking anything. No liquid. No gagging over a blender at six in the morning.

I almost scrolled past it. I had a bathroom cabinet full of expensive failures and I wasn't eager to add another one.

But I kept coming back to what my cousin had said. Three problems. Three solutions. And this was the only thing I'd found that addressed all three in one place. The motility piece. The sulfur piece. The fiber piece. Not a laxative. Not a colon cleanse. Something designed to work upstream, where my problem actually was.

I ordered a bottle. I didn't tell anyone. I didn't want to explain another supplement. Another hope. Another thing that probably wouldn't work.

Two gummies every morning. That was the dosage.

The first three days, nothing happened. I almost threw them away.

Day four, I noticed something small. I burped after lunch — just a regular burp. No sulfur. No rotten-egg taste. Just... air. I actually paused. I couldn't remember the last time a burp didn't make me want to hide.

I told myself it was coincidence.

Day seven, I woke up and something was different. The brick was lighter. Not gone — but lighter. Like someone had taken ten pounds off the cinder block sitting in my upper stomach. I ate half a banana and could feel it moving. Actually moving. Not sitting. Not fermenting. Moving.

By the end of week two, I went to the bathroom. A real one. Not rabbit pellets. Not concrete. Not the kind where you're gripping the counter and praying. Just... normal. The kind I used to have before all of this started.

I sat there and cried. Not from pain. From relief.

Week three, my husband and I went to dinner. At a restaurant. I ordered grilled chicken and vegetables. I ate slowly. I waited for the brick. I waited for the sulfur. I waited for the moment where I'd have to excuse myself and sit in a stall calculating whether I could make it through dessert.

It didn't come.

We sat there for two hours. I had coffee after the meal — something I hadn't done in months because the liquid used to push me over the edge. I drove home with the windows down and didn't think about my stomach once.

My sister came to visit the following weekend. She stopped mid-sentence in my kitchen and looked at me.

"You look different," she said.

"I lost weight," I started.

"No, not that. You look... lighter. Like something let go."

I told her everything. The side effects. The months of silence. The three problems. What I'd been taking.

She grabbed my arm. "Send me the link tonight. My friend Deborah has been on Mounjaro since March and she's miserable."

I sent it. Deborah ordered it the next morning. Three weeks later she texted my sister a photo of herself at a restaurant. Smiling. Plate half-eaten. Caption: "First dinner out in four months."

By week six, I had my follow-up with my doctor. She asked how the side effects were going. I told her the truth — the sulfur burps had stopped, I was going to the bathroom regularly, and the brick feeling had faded to almost nothing.

She looked surprised. "What changed?"

I told her about the three-part approach. Upstream motility support. Chlorophyll for the sulfur. Soluble fiber instead of bulk. I told her about the celery juice supplement I'd found — called Motilli — that combined all three.

She wrote the name down. "The side effects are the number one reason people quit these medications. If this is helping you stay on it without suffering, that matters."

It does matter. That's what I want you to understand.

Motilli isn't a laxative. It doesn't force anything. It works upstream — on the stomach, not the colon. It neutralizes the sulfur gas that makes you afraid to open your mouth in public. And it softens things with a gentle fiber instead of making the blockage worse.

I take two gummies every morning with my coffee. That's it.

The weight is still coming off. The food noise is still silent. But now I can eat dinner without dread. I can answer the phone without calculating burp risk. I can sleep through the night.

I got the miracle back. The whole miracle.

If you're sitting where I was — on the edge of a bathtub at 2 AM, wondering if the weight loss is worth what it's costing you — I need you to hear what I wish someone had told me months ago.

You don't have to choose. You don't have to trade your social life for a smaller dress size. You don't have to suffer in silence while everyone tells you how amazing you look.

Your family needs you present at the table, not locked in the bathroom. Your body needs something that works where the problem actually is — upstream, in the stomach, not downstream in the colon. And you need something you can actually take every day without gagging, without drinking sixteen ounces of liquid your stomach can't handle, without adding one more complicated routine to a life that already feels held together with rubber bands.

Motilli is what I found. It gave me my life back while I kept losing weight.

I can't promise it'll do the same for you. Bodies are different. But every woman I've shared it with has come back and said the same thing: "Why didn't anyone tell me about this sooner?"

I'm telling you now.

Motilli. Two gummies. Every morning. That's where I'd start.
